speechtext: On the orders of the day;

subtopic: UNLAWFUL ACTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: should like to ask a question of the Minister of Justice. In view of the joint announcement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), and the attorney general of the province of British Columbia of a new three-point program to solve the "Sons of Freedom" Doukhobor problem; and in view of a press report that the attorney general of British Columbia stated that there has been recognition by Ottawa that the Doukhobor problem amounts to civil insurrection; and in view of the great importance of this question to residents of the southern interior of British Columbia and the Canadian people, would the minister make a statement to the house with respect to this program and the degree of responsibility the government is willing to accept toward the solution of the "Sons of Freedom" Doukhobor problem, and does the dominion government consider this situation a state of civil insurrection?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: UNLAWFUL ACTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his question. May I say


first of all that one of the alleged facts upon which the hon. member's question is based is incorrect. The announcement to which he refers was not a joint statement, but one issued solely by the attorney general of British Columbia, as is clear from its opening sentence.
My hon. friend asks whether the federal government considers this Doukhobor situation a state of civil insurrection. There has been no occasion for the federal government to form an opinion on this point. The point has never been discussed between the attorney general of British Columbia and myself, and it will be noticed that in his press statement there is no allegation that the problem in question amounts to civil insurrection. Such recognition is not necessary to the planning or working out of this joint program. It has been possible for us to co-operate in an effective way without any consideration of this point.
As the statement by the Hon. Mr. Wismer indicates, we supplied Mr. F. G. Mead, a former high officer in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, as a member of a two-man committee "to advise the British Columbia government as to the action necessary to stop these crimes"-and when I use these words I am quoting from Hon. Mr. Wismer's statement. That is to say, Mr. Mead was to advise on the law enforcement aspect of the Doukhobor problem in British Columbia, which is a provincial responsibility.
At the same time Mr. Mead was to act as an adviser to our government on the custodial care of the Doukhobors in the federal penitentiaries, which is our federal responsibility. So acting he will be a liaison between the two governments to assist in harmonizing and co-ordinating provincial actions on law enforcement and federal actions with regard to the custodial care of Doukhobor prisoners in federal penitentiaries.
In this way we are managing, on a friendly and co-operative basis, to achieve a very considerable measure of co-ordination in our respective efforts. This I think will be further assisted by the fact that the British Columbia government has taken power to enter into a contract with this government to have the Royal Canadian Mounted Police look after the policing work of the province of British Columbia, as that force has been doing successfully in several other provinces for some years past.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 26, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a Canadian Press dispatch appearing in yesterday's newspapers drew attention to the fact that this budget debate has been characterized by speeches which, with few exceptions, have been related to the budget and have not strayed far afield. In the modest contribution I hope to make to this

The Budget-Mr. Fleming debate this afternoon I also propose to confine my remarks to the budget and matters related directly thereto.
Those who heard the budget delivered in this house by the minister several weeks ago must have found it impossible to refrain from contrasting the speech, its proposals, and the manner of its delivery with the efforts of the same minister one year ago. Gone on this occasion was the debonair manner, the air of confidence, which characterized the speech and manner of the minister in 1949. This was a gloomy, sober occasion in 1950. The speech was gloomy; the manner of delivery was indeed sober; and the final paragraph in which, before concluding, the minister sought to arouse a faint cheer, was in striking contrast to the manner with which he approached his task. In 1949 the minister's mood was to give anything that was asked. The 1950 mood was to refuse everything. Indeed, the only resemblance between the Minister of Finance in 1949 and the Minister of Finance in 1950 was the fact that, as I read in the press, he wore the same suit on both occasions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Another economy measure.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How the Minister of Finance reconciles the note struck in his budget speech with the vaunted optimism, more accurately described as flights of fancy, in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is wont to indulge with enthusiasm generated for political occasions, yet remains to be determined.
The Minister of Finance has grown up in a political school which has attached great importance to timing. As a matter of fact, following his budget speech in 1949 he permitted himself to say something on this subject for the guidance of future generations. A Canadian Press dispatch appearing in the newspapers of March 24, 1949, pictures the scene following the delivery of the give-away election budget. It pictures the Minister of Finance making his triumphant withdrawal from the chamber and his triumphant entry into the government lobby. It speaks about the members gathering around him, cheering, shaking his hand one after the other, Mr. King among them. Then the report goes on:
Mr. Abbott grinned1, took off the big brown-rimmed glasses and rocked from foot to foot on his heels, as he does.
He looked across the faces at the retired Prime Minister and said, "As Mr. King says, boys, the timing of what you do can be just as important as the thing you're doing."
The lesson in timing in 1949 will not have been lost on those members of this house who owe their presence here to the donations made for their benefit by the Minister


of Finance on that occasion; but this year the Canadian taxpayer has looked in vain for the same delicate sense of timing that characterized the speech of the minister one year ago.
The Canadian taxpayer, who is a pretty sound individual, will be applying a little of his common sense to this doctrine of timing. He will not have forgotten, of course, that 1949 was the election year, and the minister was prepared to "shoot the works", as he did. In 1950 we find the cupboard bare, because this is not an election year. In this budget speech the Minister of Finance has gone out of his way to make it abundantly clear to the Canadian taxpayer of 1950, 1951, 1952, and perhaps down as far as 1953 or 1954, that if he is expecting reductions in taxation he is doomed to disappointment. That same delicate sense of timing will dictate, in the light of what the minister has said, that any reductions in taxation shall be carefully preserved for the next preelection session of parliament, whenever that may be. The net result is that we have a complete exposure of the purpose and guiding principles of budgeting as practised by the government. It is budgeting for and by political expediency, nothing more.
Well, at times the Minister of Finance gives indications of being a realist. In a speech over the C.B.C. national network on April 11 he correctly described his own budget in these words: "It was not a popular or exciting budget." Amen, say all those who heard it. If one were to summarize the budget in a sentence, I suppose that sentence would be to this effect: the picture for the overburdened taxpayer is utterly hopeless; no reductions in taxation are possible for him.
Before I go further I wish to put in direct contrast with that attitude on the part of the government the position of the official opposition. We altogether reject the idea that expenditures and taxes cannot be reduced, and I shall endeavour to indicate some proposals that we have made and shall continue to make along these lines. We take issue with the attitude of the minister when he says in effect that it is just no use trying, so why bother making the effort to pare expenditures or reduce taxes?
Mention has been made of the subject of cyclical budgeting. In this same radio speech the minister undertook to comment on that subject. He did not know whether he had ever used that expression before, but in his speeches in the house he has certainly subscribed to the theory of cyclical budgeting; there can be no question about that. Those of us who sat in this

house in 1948 will not forget the discussions that took place at that time on the budget, when for the purpose of frightening this house and the people of Canada the minister was holding up what he pictured as the dire calamities that would follow any abandonment of the theory of cyclical budgeting. His idea then was that when times are good he should draw off that surplus of money in the pockets of the people and in that way do the people a favour, because he would be helping them out of a difficulty and helping to meet the problem of inflation. If the picture now is half as bright as that drawn by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in those flights of fancy of his, then surely this is one of those occasions for doing that	very thing.	But	the Ministerof	Finance	knows quite	well	that politicalexpediency would not permit it; that would be	equal to	an exposure	of the manoeuvresof	the 1949 budget.	The	Minister of
Finance, sir, has buried cyclical budgeting.
A word now about the position of the minister in regard to expenditures. It is fair to say that the budget speech contained more references to expenditures than previous budget speeches. As a matter of fact, it may be that the minister is at long last showing some faint indications of becoming aware that there are such things, and aware of the problems connected with them. I am sure this house will condemn with all its might the fatalistic acceptance of this ceiling on expenditures which the minister took for granted in his speech. We have his acceptance of a sort of inevitability of a continuing level of expenditures at $2,400 million per annum. We have, on the part of the minister and the government, a confession of helplessness, or a lack of will;
I do not know which it is.
I was brought up in Galt, a city largely populated by people of Scottish descent. I was brought up to understand that in all honourable undertakings, and particularly in matters related to money, where there is a will there is a way. It does not fit into the upbringing I had in that environment to have the minister sit back and, with this gesture of futility, say that nothing can be done about it; that we have to accept $2,400 million per annum as the inevitable floor on expenditures. Before I go any further, let me say that I join with the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) in the condemnation he offered in this house the other night of the fatalistic attitude toward so-called "uncontrollable" expenditure.
_ I go on from that, sir, to say that inherent in the minister's attitude there is something

It is not unfair-and I want to-be fair to the Minister of Finance-to say that whenever we have considered this subject of the necessity of a close examination of proposed expenditures, and the need for exercising the greatest sense of responsibility, the-attitude of the minister has been one of defiance.

The house will recall the concrete proposals made by the member tor Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), and the member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser), about the publicity expenditure of $6 million, the expenditure on sundries of $17,500,000, and travelling expenses of $26 million. I am sorry that my friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is not in the house, because I should like to refer to something that concerns him. It also concerns the government, and I hope it is a matter of concern to the house. You will remember, sir, that when the government announced in the house it was proposing to use as a residence for the Prime Minister a property which had been expropriated by the government some four or five years ago, there was no voice raised in the house in opposition to this principle of establishing a home for the Prime Minister at the expense of the nation.
I want to make it abundantly clear that, so far as I am concerned, there is no thought at all of quarrelling with the idea of acquiring proper housing accommodation for the Prime Minister at the expense of the nation. But I think this house wants to see some business principles applied to the procedure being followed by the government. I say, sir, in this respect, as well as in respect to many other matters that have been exposed in this house, the government did not follow business principles that would even do justice to the proprietor of a peanut stand.
What did we find when this subject was discussed in the house on March 21? To begin with, the minister could not remember the exact price of the land and buildings. It was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $130,000 or $140,000. I suppose $10,000 is a mere bagatelle about which they do not worry. He proceeded to tell us that he could not say what the project was going to cost; he indicated, if you please, that the government embarked upon the great expenditure they were proposing to make on this property, yet did not know before they started what they were going to spend. Is that not an amazing situation? They embarked gaily on the venture of improving this old property, but when they started they did not have any idea what the improvements were to cost them. They now say the main building is to cost, for renovation and reconstruction, probably about $135,000; they are still not sure. The improvements on the grounds will cost another $10,000, and it is not known yet what the furnishings will cost. I should like 

to make it clear that I am not condemning the acquisition of a suitable property as a residence for the Canadian Prime Minister, but I do condemn with all my heart such a wanton disregard of elementary business principles as applied to the expenditure of money on this or any other project.
In this connection hon. members will not overlook the words of the scripture to be found in the fourteenth chapter of the Gospel according to St. Luke, where this question is asked by Our Lord:
Which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?
Apparently the government is animated by other ideas.

A further example of the kind of proposal that we have put forward is that made by my leader yesterday when he urged that the duplication of services as between dominion and provinces should have the attention of the government with a view to the elimination of that duplication and the cost thereof.
Now I come to something that is, in my humble opinion, fundamental to our whole approach to this question of the elimination of extravagance and the exercise of greater responsibility in the house in the voting of public moneys. I wish to speak about the method followed in this house in relation to the review, if it ever may honestly be called such, of the estimates of expenditures. The fact of the matter is that today the method that prevails in the house is so awkward and so clumsy that it makes any proper check of expenditures impossible. The Auditor General said truly of late:
It is generally recognized that the task of reviewing estimates produces a feeling of frustration. The limited time available and the broad diversity of public services permit only a scratching of the surface.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, little more than a scratching of the surface is possible under the procedure that prevails in this house at the present time. It seems to me to be the greatest self-contradiction for the minister to be hurling defiance at the opposition to put forward concrete proposals, as we have been doing even in the face of handicaps, while at the same time he insists upon defeating every effort we have made to devise a method that will make possible a proper and adequate review of the estimates.
What is possible? There was a time when it was at least an expression of wish on the part of Liberal leaders in the house that the house might find the kind of method that I am speaking of, a method that does not prevail today, even by faint resemblance. It

was no less a person than Mr. W. L. Mackenzie King who in this house in 1928, in a debate in which the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Bennett, had put forward the same kind of plea that I am making here today, said, as reported at page 4048 of Hansard of that year:
I entirely agree with my hon. friend that the system at present in force, under which a minister of the crown is necessarily dependent in the House of Commons on his deputy for much of the needed information, with the deputy also of necessity, often not wholly familiar with all the details of particular branches, is most unsatisfactory. Speaking for the government I would say that we would welcome a change in the present method, a change which would not only afford fuller opportunity for discussion but which would carry with it an obligation on the part of the heads of different branches of the public service to appear before a committee of the house and explain fully the reasons which have occasioned the recommendations which find their place in the estimates submitted to the house.
Those were the words of Mr. Mackenzie King in 1928.

If civil servants, who recommend amounts to ministers, know they may be subjected to direct questioning by parliamentarians, they will put forward only such amounts as they can readily justify.
Mr. King's deliverances on the subject did not end there. As late as 1944 we find him delivering himself of similar sentiments. In that year I was not a member of the house, but it happens that-

The Budget-Mr. Fleming of the recommendations, if you please, was that there should not be a committee on estimates. What did Mr. King do about the report of the committee? The Budget-Mr. Fleming

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The speech was made to a group of women, the University Women's Club, and the report reads in part as follows:
Mr. Abbott told the women his first step in its drafting-
That is, of the budget.
-was consideration of the nation's revenue position. This done, he requested and eventually got departmental estimates, which were invariably higher than their need.
That is a most interesting comment on the part of the minister as to the way in which these estimates begin their course.
I think it is worth recalling also that when the Auditor General made an appearance before the public accounts committee in 1949, he was questioned on this subject of a cushion in the estimates, and also about the desirability of having a detailed examination by members of the house of officials who have submitted those estimates-not insulated by some minister who holds whispered conferences with the official at the desk in front of him, and then raises his head and gives the house secondhand information. At page 42 of the proceedings of the standing committee on public accounts of 1949 we find this interesting passage. Mr. Watson Sellar says:
The Witness: In every vote a department puts in a cushion and the smaller the vote the bigger is the cushion, relatively speaking.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is a pretty small cushion in my riding.
I do not know whether that is the one he sits on, sir, or not. The report continues:
The Witness: When I was in the treasury I could run salary costs of a staff of 1,000 people at one per cent less than the amount which I asked from parliament because I would have during the year sufficient resignations, deaths, and casualties of one sort and another that I had a cushion actually within my total. Therefore, I say that when a vote is mainly a salary vote you do not need a cushion of more than one per cent or one and one-half per cent, if it is a fairly large vote. If you have a lot of small votes you are going to put in a cushion of five per cent to ten per cent and therefore you are voting more money than is actually needed. You can see that by the amounts which lapse. When we apply to the treasury board for estimates they ask us how much we spent last year and if we can show that we spent every cent we have an argument which is accepted in our favour. Therefore we may have spent money we did not actually need just because we had a margin.
It is no answer for the minister to say: Oh, well, if they are lapsed, these moneys are not spent because this enters into the preparation of the estimates and the planning of expenditures. I am recorded further down on the page as asking this question:

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask Mr. Sellar a question about this matter of the cushion? Do you find it general practice in estimating to set up cushions on all items?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course it is.

He has been raised in this school which flourishes on the treasury benches. He knows that the practice of setting up cushions prevails. I continue with the quotation:
The Witness:	We will never admit, sir, that we
have a cushion in, but we all put cushions in.
By Mr. Fleming:
Q. To what extent do these cushions exist?-A. You can go by the lapsings. That is what you have to go by to see the real cushion. As a rule it will rim anywhere from two per cent to five cent of the votes.
Q. Your recommendation with regard to showing in the estimates the actual expenditure for the last year is made because you feel you can eliminate those cushions, or reduce them?-A. No. There is nothing which scares civil servants more than to face criticism from the House of Commons, and if you have actual figures to criticize us upon we are more vulnerable than when you have got to pull figures out of the air.
Now, sir, there is some pretty good common sense there for hon. members to follow if they seriously want to tackle this problem of eliminating extravagance and unnecessary expenditures. Mr. Watson Sellar has made concrete proposals about the revamping of the form of the estimates, a drastic revamping of the form in order that hon. members may have before them more and more information when they are called upon to vote these moneys. I am sure it will not escape the knowledge of the house that what are called "details" in the estimates have no statutory effect whatsoever. They do not become part of the Appropriation Act. It is high time, sir, that there was a complete revamping of the form in which estimates are submitted to the house, and that the suggestions, the very useful suggestions, put forward by the Auditor General, not on one occasion only but on many occasions, should be adopted.
This subject was before the public accounts committee in 1947, and that committee made a recommendation to the house, which is to be found at page 752 of the Journals of the house for that year. This is part of the report of the committee received by the house on July 9, 1947. There are two recommendations only that I shall quote. First:
Your committee is also of the opinion that consideration should be given by the government to amending the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, in the light of Mr. Sellar's memorandum dated July 3, 1947, supplementing the oral evidence given by him on July 2.
And further:
Your committee is also of the opinion that the house should explore the desirability of establishing a standing committee on estimates.
That suggestion, sir, has been before the house on subsequent occasions, and the Minister of Finance has objected to it. What valid reason can there be for denying to the

house a sensible procedure which would give hon. members sitting on that committee an opportunity of conducting a detailed review of the estimates, and an examination of the officials who are responsible for the preparation of those estimates, so that they would be in a position to make proper reports to the house? It would save the time of the house, and it would enable the house, by a sensible procedure, to discharge a responsibility which rests upon it, but which, sir, is not discharged by this house today, and cannot be discharged as long as we are left to flounder around under an antiquated, clumsy, awkward procedure.
There is one further concrete suggestion that I put alongside those that I have already made this afternoon. It has to do with the subject of national development, because national development, as you will recall, sir, plays a leading part in the amendment put before the house by my leader. The reason for recommending this policy of national development is that not only will it increase the prosperity of the people, extend employment, help this country to meet the still serious problem of unemployment, and help the people to raise the standard of living, but it will also enable the country, in respect of its public business operated through parliament and the government, to sustain overhead.
An unusually heavy overhead of government has been built up in this country. We have such an overhead as would not have to be greatly increased if we had a substantial increase in population. For instance, when we are called upon to vote large amounts of money to meet the deficits on the Canadian National Railways, we know perfectly well that with a larger population and a higher volume of traffic moving there would be smaller deficits to bear, and overhead on that account would be reduced. There are other examples that one could cite.
There is the subject of national defence. If we had a substantial increase in population, a larger population helping to carry the load of overhead, the amount required for defence would not be correspondingly increased. These are things that represent today a relatively fixed overhead. An increase in population would not tend to increase it, but would help us who are here today to carry it. Therefore, sir, this subject of national development is one of first importance, both in relation to the prosperity of the country, and in enabling the country to carry the load of expenditures to the extent required to meet necessary government services.
The Budget-Mr. Fleming
There were some other subjects and other concrete proposals I had hoped to make to the house, but I see that my time is almost up, and I shall have to reserve them for the committee stage.
Sir, I shall conclude these remarks by saying that I hope the house will not sit back and simply be content to share that demonstration of fatalistic acceptance of the burden of taxation, the heavy load of expenditures, which has been exhibited on the part of the Minister of Finance. Surely, in a red-blooded country like this, inhabited by an intelligent people, we can muster in this house-if the government will not continue to sit on the lid and attempt to thwart the efforts of the house to devise a proper method of reviewing expenditures and grappling with this problem of high taxes and high expenditures-surely we can muster enough intelligence, given that opportunity, to cope with this problem, and to give some relief to the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I decided to speak this afternoon I did not know that I would have the pleasure of speaking after the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). Before continuing with the remarks that I had prepared I should like to say a few words about some of the things the hon. member has said. I was greatly amused and interested in the comparison he made between the budgets of 1949 and 1950.
I should like to remind him that one cannot reduce taxes every year as the government did in 1949. If that were done, pretty soon there would not be any taxes left. Let me tell my hon. friend that every day cannot be a Sunday. There are certain years when the government can afford to reduce taxes, there are other years when they cannot afford to do so. It depends upon the condition of the affairs of the country and the state of the national income; if
1938	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Cannon depends upon the expenditures the government has been obliged to make in the past but can afford to reduce.
It so happened that in 1949 there were many of the heavy expenditures that had resulted from the war that had reached the point where they could be reduced. The national income had reached a higher level and the government was able to make substantial reductions in taxation.
' My hon. friend insinuated that those reductions were made simply because it was an election year. I assure him that he is being led into error by pure coincidence. It just so happened that the situation that year was such that it was possible to reduce taxes.
My hon. friend also said something about the expenditures being made on the house being renovated as a residence for the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). There we have another example of the kind of opposition we are having in the house. The opposition has been saying to us session after session, "We like what you are doing, we are for it, but we do not like the way you are doing it." That is all the criticism the opposition has been able to make. I submit that it is a mark in favour of the government and its policies in general that the only criticism the opposition is able to make is about methods and not about facts or principles. As to the amount being spent on the residence for the Prime Minister I would ask my hon. friend-I am sorry to see he is leaving-whether he has ever had to repair an old house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I must go to the public accounts committee.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member can read my remarks in Hansard. I am sure there are many hon. members who have had personal experience with repairing an old house or who have friends who have had this experience. They know that it is practically impossible to tell what a job like that will cost when you start to do it. You must wait until it is finished to know the exact cost. This is due to the inherent nature of the work to be done. Something is pulled down and you find that something else has to be repaired. It is physically impossible to determine beforehand exactly how much a job like that is going to cost.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Better to tear down the old house and build a new one.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was suggested during the debate in the house. No doubt it would have cost a lot more than to do the job now being


done. Let me say to the house and particularly to the members of the opposition that they need not worry about the way the job is going to be done. The Department of Public Works and the Liberal government will do a good job on this as they have done on other things they have undertaken in the past.
The hon. member of Eglinton during the course of his remarks said that one of the reasons why the estimates were not submitted to a committee was that the government was afraid Liberal members might consider they had greater latitude in committee and might be more difficult to control there than they would be when speaking in the house. I am pleased to be able to say to the hon. member for Eglinton and to other members of the opposition that no Liberal member is censored by anybody as to what he is to say. He gets up and speaks and there is no control over what he wants to say. It was insinuated that our esteemed whip had something to do with it, but I can assure you, as the house probably knows, that the only thing the whip does is to decide who is going to speak and in what order the speeches will be made.
I simply wanted to develop a few notes that I made while the hon. member for Eglinton was speaking. I shall leave the substance of his speech to the minister concerned; I know he will know how to deal with it if he can find any substance in it.
As the member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine I want to take advantage of this opportunity to thank the government for the amounts that have been included in the estimates this year to cover work in my county. There are several suggestions that I intend to make later on. An amount has been included in the estimates for the building of a breakwater at Etang du Nord. Etang du Nord is on a bay on the north side of the island. This bay is frequented by a great number of fishermen but for some time fishing has been difficult because of changed conditions. This bay used to be sheltered from the north wind and seas by a natural breakwater formed by a cape. That cape has been slowly eaten away by the waves and for some years the fishermen have had no protection. The bay has been gradually filling up with sand and they are not able to bring in their boats as far as they used to. For some time they have been asking the government to build a breakwater to replace the natural one that disappeared. I am glad to be able to tell them that finally their requests have been recognized by this government as being well founded and that the necessary amount is included in the estimates to build this breakwater.

Another important item of public works for which the government has provided in the estimates is on Hospital bay. Hospital bay is also on the north side of the island and is exposed to the north wind and the high seas. There is a natural lagoon deep enough and large enough to provide shelter for the fishing boats, but unfortunately it is separated from the sea by a sandbar. An amount is included in the estimates this year to dig a channel through the sandbar. This channel will be lined with steel stanchions which will provide a permanent channel. The fishermen will then be able to get the necessary protection from the elements. This public work has been demanded for a great many years by the fishermen of my county and I am glad to be able to thank the government in their name for including this item in the estimates.
Unfortunately the people of my county will not be so pleased with the estimates of the Department of Transport. The Department of Transport is in charge of the building of airstrips. During the year the main means of transportation for passengers between the islands and the mainland is by air. Aircraft take off from Charlottetown twice a week for the islands, and there they land on a sandbar. While they have been landing on the sandbar for some years, the fact remains that Maritime Central Airways render a good service. They have excellent pilots, and I wish to congratulate them upon the service they are giving. However, we know it is better to land on a landing strip than to land on a sandbar.
Last year an amount of $25,000 was set aside to build a landing strip on Amherst island, and also $25,000 to build another landing strip on Grindstone island, which is the main island in the group. Grindstone and Amherst islands are the islands upon which the greater part of the population live. Last year the $25,000 was used in connection with the airstrip on Amherst island, and that work was completed, with the exception of the surfacing. An extra amount of $10,000 would be required for surfacing, but unfortunately that amount is not included in the estimates. It is very necessary that it should be spent this year, because the surface of the airstrip is soft, and when it rains, or when the weather is mild, the airstrip cannot be used. In the autumn and also in the spring of the year there are long periods of time when it is completely out of use.
Therefore I take this opportunity of asking the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), in the name of my electors, to see whether 55946-124
The Budget-Mr. Cannon it would not be possible to find $10,000- I am told it would require that amount-to finish that airstrip.
There was also voted last year an amount for the airstrip at Grindstone island. Because of difficulties with the municipal corporation in connection with the site of the airstrip, the contract was not signed and the money was not spent. As all hon. members know, after March 31, that money was lost, so far as its expenditure was concerned. I am told now however that the municipality has found another location which would be satisfactory to them. They are now ready to sign an agreement, and I would ask that this $25,000 be included in the estimates for this year. Grindstone island is the main island, and it would be of great help to my electors if we could have an airstrip at that point. If that were done we would not have to' continue to make landings on the sandbar to which I have already referred.
I wish also to thank the government for having asked me to serve on the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on old age security. I realize this is an important committee. It is important to all the electors in Canada, and particularly to those in my county. Eighty-five per cent of those people are fishermen, and are engaged in a difficult and hazardous profession. They cannot continue fishing in their old age; and as a certain number of them are invalids social security is important to them. Therefore I thank the government for having placed me on the committee, and I assure my electors that I shall do my best to act in their interests and to see that social security is developed as it should be.
In that connection I should like to say a word about pensions for invalids. In this country we have no pensions for invalids. In the literature I have read in connection with my work in the committee on old age security I have found that in several other countries they have pensions for invalids, people who are unable to earn their own living. Those pensions are tied up with old age security programs. I suggest the time has come when this country might also give its attention to the question of giving pensions to invalids. We give pensions to the blind, a procedure of which I am very much in favour. I am sure however that every hon. member knows that in every constituency there are a certain number of invalids who are just as incapable of earning a living as are the blind people. I believe we should extend the principle, and see what can be done by way of social security for these poor invalids.

The Budget-Mr. Cannon
A resolution now stands on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand) which deserves the support of hon. members who have similar problems in their constituencies. It should be impressed upon the government that the time has now come to do something about giving pensions to invalids.
May I take this opportunity also to congratulate the government upon the good work that has been done for the fishermen and the fishing industry generally by the fisheries prices support board. I have had occasion to deal with that board several times since coming to the House of Commons, and I must say I have always found them most helpful and co-operative. I believe they are doing excellent work within the scope of the powers given to them. I submit however that the scope of their powers is not wide enough.
The fishing industry in our country has become very important indeed, particularly in view of the fact that we now have Newfoundland as our tenth province. At least seven provinces are vitally interested in the fishing industry. There are, of course, Newfoundland, the three maritime provinces, Quebec, also Manitoba because of the extensive fishing industry in lake Winnipeg, and the province of British Columbia. When seven provinces in our country are vitally interested in the fishing industry, then I say the government ought to do as much for that industry, on a smaller scale of course, as it does for agriculture. The organizations having to do and dealing with fishing ought to have the same scope of action as those which deal with agriculture.
We find in the statutes of 1944-1945 the Agricultural Prices Support Act. In the same statutes we find the Fisheries Prices Support Act. These two statutes are practically identical. The powers of the boards as set out in them are, briefly, to prescribe from time to time, with the approval of the governor in council, prices at which the board may purchase agricultural or fisheries products on the market. The Agricultural Prices Support Act then sets out this further power:
To purchase at such prices any agricultural product, if such product, on inspection, meets standards as to grade and quality-
And so on. The corresponding statute dealing with fisheries contains a similar provision. The statute dealing with agriculture continues:
To sell or otherwise dispose of any agricultural product purchased by the board.
Then there is in both statutes a provision to make up the deficiency between prices set by the boards, as the prices the producers
[Mr. Cannon.)

should receive, and those prices they actually do receive, both for agricultural and fisheries products. The provisions in the Agricultural Prices Support Act continue:
To package, process, store, ship, transport, export or insure any agricultural product.
Then there is the provision permitting the board to enter into contracts, and this further provision:
To purchase at market or contract prices and export any agricultural product under any contract between His Majesty in right of Canada and any other government or agency thereof and to do all things necessarily incidental thereto.
And there is a similar provision concerning fisheries. These two statutes were passed in 1944. Evidently in 1947 the government felt it had not gone far enough in connection with agricultural products, with the result that it passed in that year the Agricultural Products Act. The long title is "An Act to Provide for the Sale and Export of Agricultural Products". This statute gives the minister, subject to regulations made by the governor in council, authority to-
(a)	sell or export agricultural products to the government of any country or any agency thereof pursuant to any agreement made by the government of Canada with the government of such country or with such agency and for those purposes may purchase agricultural products and make such arrangements for the purchase, sale or export of agricultural products as he considers necessary or desirable;
(b)	on behalf of the government of any country or any agency thereof purchase or negotiate contracts for the purchase of agricultural products;
(c)	by order require any person-
That is not important.
(d)	enter into contracts for the storing or processing of agricultural products.
We all know that under the authority of that statute the government has made some very good contracts with other countries for the sale of agricultural products, which have been very helpful to our farmers. I believe we should have something similar for fisheries products. I give as an example a body that was organized and has been in existence for some time in Newfoundland; that is, the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited. This is a central body that markets all the fish caught in Newfoundland. It has done a very good job in finding and keeping markets for the fishermen of that province. Now that Newfoundland has become a part of Canada I suggest we should have a statute similar to the one I just read, which would enable the government to set up a central marketing agency for all fisheries products including those of Newfoundland. In view of the importance of the fishing industry to this country, as I have outlined it, I believe the two industries should be placed on an equal

footing. When the need arises the government should be in a position to do for the fishing industry what it now can do for the industry of agriculture.
One other subject that interests me and my electors is unemployment insurance. Fishermen are excepted under the act at the present time. Recently the government found it possible to extend the Unemployment Insurance Act to lumbermen, and I suggest that attention should be given to the possibility of also extending it to fishermen. As a first step I suggest it might be extended to fishermen's aides. Most of these people are employed on a salary basis, and that being so I submit there is no reason why they should not be permitted to contribute to the fund and draw unemployment insurance just like any other worker in Canada. I understand that in the case of fishermen not employed by anyone, who are their own masters, there are certain administrative difficulties which would make it necessary to have the act extensively amended, but in the case of fishermen's helpers who are on salary I submit that the unemployment insurance commission already has all the powers necessary. I draw this point to the attention of the government in the hope that it may be possible to do something about it.
This is about all I have to say, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion I should like to reiterate the thanks of the electors of my county for the amount that has been placed in the estimates for their benefit.
