speechtext: My friend is bound to interrupt, even when someone is making a speech which is not controversial. I recommend to the gentleman to whom the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) refers as the junior from Capilano that he cultivate the habit of keeping quiet when someone is making a speech, unless he is definitely challenging the material in that speech.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was supporting you.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know what the member was doing, but I would suggest, sir, that you keep the hon. gentleman quiet until I have finished, at which time he can make a speech of his own.
I was mentioning these excursions to Churchill and saying that some of the eastern Canadians would be amazed at some of the things they would see. I was amazed at some of the things I saw. One may see, as I did, an Eskimo child chewing a piece of frozen fish while lying on the doorstep of one of the most modern stores in western Canada,
tMr. Knight.]

containing refrigerators and all sorts of electrical equipment. Perhaps if one is a sportsman, one may be interested in ptarmigan or caribou, or may like to see the white whales playing in the harbour which, I understand, already form the basis of a small industry. As a strange contradiction one can see the finest port in the world, I mean from the point of view of a natural shelter as well as from the point of view of the artificial things, the manmade equipment that has been put there for handling grain.
If one crosses the harbour to the other shore, one finds the old Prince of Wales fort. My French-speaking confreres would be particularly interested in that fort if they would read its history. On the day I was there we were fortunate enough to be able to cross over on a little tug owned by the Department of Transport. I am afraid that the Department of Transport did not know we were doing that, because I understand the department has now prohibited the tug from carrying passengers. I asked a question about it, and received that answer. Personally, I think it is a reasonable attitude, because one could not expect a tug to be run in passenger service unless there were adequate provisions for safety, adequate insurance and so forth. Perhaps the member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) might exercise his good offices to persuade the government that it would be worth while to have some sort of vessel there to perform that particular service. It would add greatly to the pleasure of the tourists who gc. up there. I have found that one can always make oneself popular in this house by telling someone how we can get United States dollars. I do not put such great faith in dollars as some of my hon. friends, but I may tell you that some people from the United States make an excursion up there every year, and do leave a considerable amount of that commodity behind. So much for some of the things one may see.
The romance of discovery, I think, has disappeared from western Canada. When I was a boy and went out to homestead in western Canada, the cry was, "Go west, young man." We went west in that spirit of adventure to which I have alluded. The western lands have now been explored and exploited; there is no longer any unexplored part of the west. The future belongs to the north. When I say the future belongs to the north, I am thinking of various things. I am thinking of the natural resources, some of them known and I am sure many unknown. I am thinking that in that vast country there must be more than one Flin Flon, with its variety of minerals. I am thinking of the new oil

fields, and wondering if they do not extend somewhat into that northern country. I am thinking of the vast areas of land. May I say that in many of the countries from which my friends have come they have seen much worse land used for agricultural purposes than some of the vast expanses one finds contiguous to The Pas and along parts of the Hudson Bay railway, notably perhaps around Wabowden. Yes, there is the great north still to be explored, and there is a great outlet for that adventurous spirit, which was evidenced in opening up the western plains.
This question, sir, is not just a matter of the encouragement of the Hudson bay route as such, although I am sure we are interested in that. But when it comes to the whole exploration and opening up of these vast spaces in that new empire to the north, we find that the two questions are interdependent. Population is required in that north country if the Hudson bay route is ever to be a success. Population is needed in that country if it is ever to be explored and settled as it should be. There are a great number of people needed for the handling of the grain at certain times at the port of Churchill, and as my hon. friend knows that is a seasonal matter. Up to the present, grain handlers, dockers, loaders of ships-I do not know what the technical term is- have had to be brought in from other ports such as Montreal. If we had industry and population in those northern areas we would have a skilled body of personnel living there who could be used year by year when the proper shipping season comes around, without the expense of shipping them in from eastern Canada. We need that population to develop those thousands of acres of land to which I have made reference.
There is another question about the country and that is the strategic importance of this particular route. That point, of course, has been developed. It is an unfortunate thing that we must think about the necessity for defence, but indeed we must. The strategic importance of that particular route has been coming to our attention more and more in the last number of years. In a former speech I proposed that the government, in carrying out naval operations, might well find out a good deal about the geography and meteorology of Churchill if they would send some of their ships up into those waters, where they could perform their naval manoeuvres. I am glad to say that was done though to a small extent last summer. That raises the point of whether one of the necessities at Churchill now is not some sort of naval station which could be a base for such operations.
One of the drawbacks, by the way, in
The Budget-Mr. Knight building up population-this is a small point, but I think I will mention it here as I go along-is that it is impossible to own land in the townsite of Churchill. I was talking to some of the townspeople up there, particularly to one young man and his wife who were building their own house. They were greatly distressed that they were not able to own the land upon which their house was being built. It appears that one can get only a lease for one year. Those who have had anything to do with mortgage companies and real estate people will know that that is not a good basis upon which to raise a loan if you want to build yourself a house.
As I said, from time to time in the last five years I have made a speech or two in this house upon this Hudson bay route. I did so in 1945, in 1947, and in 1949, and I again made a short reference to it when the supplementary estimates were being considered in March of this year. I am not going to cover today the arguments which I put forward in those speeches. They were documented. The figures are there and anyone who is interested in the subject can look them up. My intention was merely to give a few general ideas.
There is no doubt in my mind that the greater use of this route and port would be beneficial to the farmers contiguous to it. From statistics I know that it is beneficial to the importers of goods who use that port as an importing point. I know that it was a benefit to Britain in buying wheat through that port. At the moment there is some controversy as to whom there is the greater benefit and I think it is largely due to the ambiguity or, shall I say, the vagueness of the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) some time ago. There is some doubt as to whether the western farmer or the importing countries will benefit the more from the making of the port of Churchill into a basing point for the sale of wheat, a point which would then be on equality in that respect with Montreal and Vancouver. I do not want to go into that particular argument. It will be settled in due course. I know, however, that there is a benefit and I know that someone gets it. There can be no doubt about that.
For years there has been a deficit in the operation of this port. Those of us who are interested in it and who, I think, may say that we know something about it, believe that, in so far as any deficit is detrimental to the taxpayers of this country-and any deficit must be-such deficit could be wiped out entirely if that port were given its proper use. We have worked it out on the basis of statistics and the expert opinion-which includes
1944	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Knight that of the manager of the port, officials of the wheat pool, officials of the railways and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier)- that if we could once put fifteen million bushels of wheat through that port there would in that particular year be no deficit in connection with the port or with the railway which serves it. I want to put that statement on the record once more. To my eastern friends who at times, through a lack of knowledge about the subject, are inclined to look upon this particular project as a white elephant, I also want to say that this railroad was built not with money out of the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada but with money which was procured from the sale of western land.
As I have said, the port has never been fully used. If everybody were as anxious to see the success of that port as we in that part of the country are, and if everyone would co-operate, I believe that not merely fifteen million bushels but from twenty million to twenty-five million bushels of wheat could be put through that port in any given year. As I see it, its success depends upon the good will of four particular government agencies which I would name as the ministry of transport, the Canadian National Railways, the harbours board and the wheat board. As I say, if these four agencies were willing, anxious and enthusiastic, that port could be made a success.
I shall now mention one or two of the difficulties which the port has had to fight in the past. If you talk to westerners you -will find the distinct opinion-as to whether at is justified I shall make no assertion here /today-that one of the things that work against the success of that road is that there are certain influences in the east here which, mistakenly I think, are opposed to it through the idea that it would interfere with their particular interests. As to the five and a half million bushels that were put through there last year, or the fifteen million bushels which would be necessary to make it pay its way; or the twenty million bushels which I would advocate and which I think would make it possible to operate at a profit, may I say that after all even the twenty million bushels are only a drop in the bucket having regard to the amount of wheat that is handled for shipment out of this country through the major ports. Surely the great ports of Montreal, Halifax and Vancouver should not grudge to us prairie people the use of our own port, which is at our back door, to the extent of such a small percentage of any year's wheat crop.
I mention that as one of the difficulties. Next I shall mention the question of insurance. There has always been a prejudice
(Mr. Knight.]

against this route. There has always been a lack of investigation about the possibility of that harbour and that route. The insurance companies, who were not particularly interested in the route in any case-they would get the business whether the wheat went through Montreal or through the port of Churchill-have, I think, always been prejudiced against that road. It is true that some adjustment has been made that has been welcomed.
The insurance period has been inflexible. It has been a period of only 65 days. I have never had anybody answer this question, but I have put it on several occasions. Why should that period be an inflexible one? The weather is not inflexible. The break-up or the freeze-up in our country comes at different times of different years. Now that we have meteorological stations in the north, now that we have people on the ground, could we not get information from time to time on which flexible rather than inflexible periods could be set?
I had lunch with a captain of a Dalgleish boat in the port of Churchill a couple of years ago. He told me that it seemed rather ridiculous to him that on a beautiful sunny day, when the sea was as calm as glass, for 48 hours he had to stay outside the limits with his ship because he dared not cross that line before the date at which he could get the protection given by insurance. Practically every captain that comes in there says the same thing. Furthermore, practically every captain that comes in there speaks in favour of the port as compared with, for instance, the port of Montreal or the port of Halifax.
I shall mention one thing which comes in a smaller category. I shall not go into it. I refer to this business of diversion charges. They are one of the drawbacks connected with the use of that port. I suppose that hon. members generally will not be interested in having a definition of diversion charges. My own definition for them is money paid for services not rendered. I think I shall let it go at that. If anyone here is curious he may look the matter up.
These are some of the things I wanted to say. There is much more that could be said. One could talk for a week on this particular subject.
I should like to put before the house the main conclusion of the brief which was presented by the association of which I spoke. This brief was presented on Monday last to the Prime Minister. Before I do so I should like to mention a man up in the north country, namely, the Rev. Father Ferron. It was my privilege and pleasure to hear him speak on

the whole subject of Hudson bay and the north country in the city of Prince Albert some time ago. He is a most interesting speaker, a man who is intimately acquainted with everything in the north country, and whose services have been used by this government in various capacities, particularly in connection with giving advice on matters related to the country north of Churchill. His talk was rather in story form. If you look through it you will find that its main theme is the theme of the brief which was presented the other day by the delegates representing the Hudson Bay association. I am going to quote a line or two from Father Ferron's address, as recorded in this little pamphlet, at a meeting in the city hall in Prince Albert-on February 7, 1950. I shall quote here and there at random the things which I think may be of some interest. They are as follows:
The drastic decision of the underwriters allows ships to be along the wharf at Churchill approximately from the eighth of August until the tenth of October, both dates inclusive, which is a total of sixty-five days. Of these sixty-five days, last summer, there were twenty days when there was not one single grain ship in the harbour.
Then further down on the same page:
To render conditions worse, out of the remaining forty-five days, there were twenty-seven when there was but a single ship in the harbour, which left only eighteen days out of the sixty-five when the present harbour worked at anywhere near capacity:
These are the facts on which I have based what I have already said in the matter of this port not being used to its full capacity even during the time covered by insurance. We firmly believe that at least three weeks could be added to the length of this particular insurance season, because there are three insurance seasons at Churchill. There is the natural one, the period during which ships are physically able to sail. Then there is the captains insurance period, a little longer than the actual one, a little shorter than the natural one; then there is the insurance one which gets very small indeed. Father Ferron's conclusion is this:
I would strongly suggest that an advisory board be formed to deal with these problems. The different departments involved in our federal capital; the provincial governments interested; the wheat pool; and your association, should all have representatives on such a board. Until such time as the different efforts are consolidated through the medium of such a board, the undertaking cannot succeed. With all the dexterity possible, this board or commission should be set up. Such is our democratic way of proceeding based on common sense and our common love of our great country of Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Robertson
As a comment on that, and following along the same idea, the delegation which presented its case to the Prime Minister the other day said this:
Our submissions take the form of a respectful request that the dominion government give consideration to;
1.	The immediate appointment of a board or council under the Department of Trade and Commerce to deal with the multitude of problems surrounding the developments' of the port of Churchill and the areas and railway referred to above.
These areas with Churchill as their natural outlet might very well, in the near future, prove to be the nucleus of a separate northern province in the scheme of Canadian confederation.
2.	That if and when such a board or council be appointed, the membership of the board be drawn from various organizations such as Canadian army, navy, and air force, commercial interests, farmers' organizations, and the Hudson Bay route association.
3.	That the duties of such a board be to keep such government departments as may be concerned informed of improvements and changes required from time to time, in order to ensure the greatest possible development of the vast northland and the utmost utilization of the harbour at the port of Churchill.
To that, sir, I would add with my own voice a plea in the same direction.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In joining in this budget address, I would wish first of all to congratulate the Minister of Finance on his very able review of our national economy in his budget speech. The Minister of Finance has already presented four budgets in this house. He has proven not only that he has a knowledge of finance but that he is well acquainted with the economic situation in Canada. I believe that he has the confidence of the people of Canada, and I hope that he will continue to bring down such satisfactory budgets in the future.
This budget was well received by the people of Canada. It represented a continuation of the sound financial policy which was undertaken by the government during the war. During the war the government adopted a "pay as you go" policy. Taxes were kept high, and as a result the threat of inflation was largely controlled.
During the war we had a far-sighted program of price control, and as a result the transition from war to peace was uneventful. Price controls have been removed, without any great disruption of our national economy. Today we are approaching a more normal period, but we are still enjoying great prosperity in Canada. Of course, no matter what our financial policies may be, no matter how great our prosperity may be, we cannot please the members of the Conservative opposition. Last year tax reductions amounting to $323 million were announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) but the members of the opposition called it bribery. Then in the next
1946	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Robertson breath they said that the bribe was not big enough. Today they say that this is a defeatist budget, but I consider it was a most able presentation of the present situation in Canada. I can see no signs of defeatism in the budget; rather, to me it indicated optimism through and through.
When we consider the fortunes of our friends of the opposition during the last fifteen years, their successes in the last election and their prospects for the future, we must agree that it does not tend toward optimism. But I would ask them not to link the fortunes of our country with the fortunes of their political party. For years we have been hearing this cry of despair from the members of that group, and yet prosperity in Canada continues. The financial critic of the opposition criticized the government for not developing our natural resources, and then in the next breath he spoke of how we were obtaining $100 million of scarce United States dollars through the development of Alberta oil-just another example of the inconsistency of members of the opposition.
I am sure that all hon. members of the house favour the development of our natural resources, but we want that development to take into consideration the ability of our economy to absorb it. We do not want to be wasteful of our resources because we shall need them in the years to come.
I listened this afternoon while the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) covered a great many subjects. He questioned what he referred to as the billion dollar philosophy of this government. Does he not realize that Canada is expanding rapidly and that the running of our country demands huge expenditures? We must talk in billions. That is one example of the great prosperity of our country. Evidently those figures overtax the hon. member for Eglinton. I judged that to be the case by his remarks on the budget.
I believe Canada's economy is in a strong position and I base that statement on certain examples I shall give. In the first place our capital investment is high, being five per cent over the record of 1949. There has been a marked improvement in our foreign reserves. From a low of $401 million in 1947 they have increased to $1,200 million at the end of March. Wages are still high. It is true we still have some unemployment, but I am prepared to accept the statement of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) that this condition will soon be improved. If it is not, then I believe that all levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal, should join together in a program to alleviate this condition. But for the present I am prepared to


accept the word of the Minister of Labour that this condition will soon be satisfactorily dealt with.
While our trade is not at the level of a few months ago, it is still satisfactory. We know the British people are short of dollars and cannot buy what they might like to buy from us if they had sufficient dollars. The Minister of Finance has pointed out that our exports to the United States have increased more than our exports to the United Kingdom have decreased. Taking the over-all picture I think we can conclude that our trade position is not too unsatisfactory.
We have a balanced budget and in these days that is an outstanding achievement. I ask hon. members to compare our budget with the budgets of the United States. For four years we have had balanced budgets while in the United States there has been a huge deficit each year. I understand that at this time it is in the nature of $7,000 million. Surely when we compare our economy with the economy of the United States there is no reason to conclude that conditions in Canada are unsatisfactory. I would point to the great reduction in our national debt which has taken place during the past four years when I believe the national debt of our country was reduced by approximately $2,000 million. That is an indication of how stable our economy is today.
I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to tell the house something of my own county of Northumberland. As many hon. members know, Northumberland county lies in central Ontario on the north shore of lake Ontario. Its western boundary is almost at the town of Port Hope and it extends eastward to the boundary of the town of Trenton. Going north the western border reaches Rice lake, and then the boundary of the constituency travels along the southern shore of Rice lake and the Trent canal to and beyond the town of Campbellford. From that point it takes a southerly direction to the town of Trenton.
Northumberland county is noted for the beauty of its towns and countryside, for the fertility of its fields and for the prosperity and high qualities of its citizens. Many hon. members who have driven through Northumberland county have mentioned the many attributes that it possesses. At the last redistribution the township of Monaghan South was added to the county of Northumberland. Previous to that time it had been in the constituency of Peterborough West. I am sure that all citizens of the county of Northumberland welcomed the addition to the township of Monaghan South.

The basic industry in Northumberland county is agriculture. I would say that approximately one-half the citizens of Northumberland county are engaged in agriculture. Mixed farming predominates in Northumberland county, but dairying is an important branch of agriculture. We have many fine dairy herds in the county of Northumberland. We ship a great quantity of fresh milk to Toronto and there is large butter production. I have been told that Seymour township, which lies in the northeast corner of the county of Northumberland, is the largest producer of cheese of any township in Canada.
Our herds have been tuberculosis tested and we are an approved area. It is therefore possible for our farmers to ship cattle to the United States and receive very high prices for them. We have fine beef herds in the county of Northumberland. I have heard certain hon. members state that their constituencies have the finest beef herds in the Dominion of Canada, but I know that they have never tasted a steak from one of the beef cattle from Northumberland county.
Northumberland county produces a great many hogs; I believe it is one of the largest producers of hogs in Ontario. Poultry is an important industry in our county, not only as a branch of agriculture but also as a commercial proposition. We are proud of the fruit and vegetable production in Northumberland county. A great many canning crops such as peas, tomatoes, corn, et cetera, are produced and there are many canning factories distributed over Northumberland county.
I believe we produce the finest apples in the Dominion of Canada. I think the McIntosh and Northern Spy apples grown in Northumberland county can outdo even the wonderful apples of the Fraser valley.
We have two large towns in Northumberland. Cobourg, the largest of these, is my home town, and one of which I am very proud. It is considered to be one of the most beautiful towns in Ontario and is, in fact, one of the oldest in the whole of Canada. I have been told, and American tourists have said for many years, that we in Cobourg have the finest ozone to be found anywhere on the whole of the North American continent. And if anyone asks me what I mean by that, I would say it is my understanding that it means the health-giving properties of the atmosphere.
The second largest town in Northumberland is Campbellford, a very beautiful town lying across the Trent river in the northeastern part of the county. It is surrounded
The Budget-Mr. Robertson by Seymour township which, I believe, is one of the most productive agricultural communities in Ontario.
In my county we have many diversified industries. I believe we have the largest plastics company in the whole of * Canada, located at Cobourg. We have several tanneries, some foundries, gun manufacturing industries, to mention but a few of them. All these industries are successful and lend much stability to Northumberland county. We have developed there a very thriving tourist trade. Being situated on lake Ontario, and having Rice lake and its connecting waters to the north, we have a perfect haven for American tourists in Canada. Each year they come in increasing numbers to enjoy the great beauties of our county.
Northumberland county has many service clubs, each of which is carrying on its own particular work of social service in the community. They take great interest in all community affairs, and the life of the county is made much richer by the activities of these clubs.
Prominent among the clubs in Cobourg is the Cobourg branch of the Canadian federation of business and professional women's clubs. As may be known to some hon. members, the business and professional women's clubs are organized internationally in nineteen countries of the world, having local groups within the United States and throughout Canada.	.
Among the objectives of this organization are the following: (1) to promote the interests of business and professional women throughout Canada; (2) to encourage a spirit of cooperation among the business and professional women in Canada; and (3) to extend occupational opportunities to business and professional women through industrial, scientific and vocational activities.
The Cobourg branch was formed in 1946 and has a present membership of 115. It was honoured by being made host for the second provincial conference of clubs which was held in Cobourg in October of 1948. Within the town the club has been very interested in civic affairs and matters of government generally. There is a standing committee of the club known as a municipal research committee, whose duty it is to keep members informed on municipal affairs within the local municipality. Of interest to hon. members of the house will be the activities of this club in connection with certain of its meetings. On April 16, 1947, the club sponsored a meeting of industry and labour in the town of Cobourg, and obtained the attendance of Mr. R. A. Wilson, field representative of
1948	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Robertson the federal Department of Labour. This meeting was widely attended and, from the point of view of the Department of Labour, was such a success in fostering better understanding and co-operation between the groups that on JVlarch 6 of this year, at the request of the officials of that department, a second similar meeting was arranged.
Of interest to members of the house will be the work of that club in assisting new Canadians. There is a committee of the club whose work it is to advise and help new Canadians resident in Cobourg. On coming to the town the chairman of the committee gets in touch with these girls, and the committee stands ready to assist in any problem the girls might have. Members of the club are to be congratulated upon their accomplishments and their influence in fostering and developing a better and broader sense of Canadianism.
In the county of Northumberland, as in other parts of Canada, organized labour plays its full part. We have in Cobourg an allied labour council composed of representatives of all the unions in the town, which meet regularly and discuss conditions as they exist in Cobourg. I believe these men compose a fine body of citizens. They are ever zealous of the true rights of labour, but still they also know their responsibilities to the community. I am glad to say that the splendid labour relations which have existed in Canada are found in my own county of Northumberland. I think all hon. members will agree that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has done much to bring about this better understanding between the various groups in Canada.
I would also bring to the attention of the house the fact that on the outskirts of Cobourg we have the most noted exponent of ceramic art in Canada. He is Mr. Jarko Zavi, who came from Czechoslovakia to Canada just before the opening of the last war. May I read to the house an article which tells something of this art:
In 1939, after the German army had marched into Prague, Jarko Zavi, ceramic artist, left his native Czechoslovakia, and came to Canada. A few years ago ceramic art in Canada was practically unknown and non-existent. People had become aware that Canada had her own painters, poets, composers and sculptors. In the home, however, most of the ceramic objects were ornaments from foreign countries which expressed the character of those countries, and about which very few Canadians knew anything . . . The war has brought many European artists and craftsmen to Canada. Because Canada has not yet a history in this art, these artists should be encouraged to transfer their knowledge to young Canadians. I do not see any reason why this cannot be done, for Canada is rich in material for ceramic modelling. We have our harvesters, miners, lumberjacks, trappers, fishermen, Eskimos and Indians; we


have horses, buffalo, Rocky Mountain goats, deer, wild geese. These are bases from which to guide our imagination. We do not have to try to force ourselves to model a Chinese figure or to make an Egyptian jug on the potter's wheel.
We in the county of Northumberland are proud of Mr. Jarko Zavi, and welcome him to our county.
I note that social security payments have been increased by $62 million to a total of $457 million this year. These sums are spent for old age pensions, family allowances and unemployment insurance. I for one am happy to support such a vast expenditure. Old age pensions and unemployment insurance give a new sense of security to the people of Canada. Family allowances give to the children of Canada a better opportunity to enjoy the full benefits of life in Canada. In my opinion the greatest single achievement of the Liberal party has been its social security program. How fortunate it has been for Canada that the Liberal party has had power for so long, in order to fully develop this program. I often wonder how much of our present program would have been developed had our Conservative friends been in power. We know the inconsistencies of the supporters of the Conservative party with regard to social security.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Page the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch).

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You know all about it, now. In this house we hear impassioned pleas from members of the Conservative party for social security; yet at the same time we read articles in the leading Conservative newspaper in Ontario criticizing this government for some of its social security plans and advising against any further extension of that program. Had our friends of the C.C.F. been in power I do not know what would have happened. Probably they would have rushed ahead with some program without properly laying the foundation, without due consideration for its cost, and I am sure the whole program would have ended in confusion. I believe that is one thing we cannot disregard, for there is nothing more important to the success of our social security program than that we have public support for it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The public are away ahead of you.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is what you think. I am confident the government made a wise decision in setting up the special committee on old age security. This study should reveal much, and I am sure the committee will be able to offer the government a great deal of help in formulating a policy to be followed in future. I should like to re-echo what was

said by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) in presenting that motion: we aim to devise the simplest, most effective and most humane system of social security it is possible for us to develop, having in mind our over-all social security responsibilities, other government responsibilities, and the ability of the country to pay. I sincerely believe that the production of this country and its vast resources permit a great liberalization of our old age security program. Great as have been the social benefits, there is an added value which I am sure is well recognized by all hon. members. The huge sums of money paid out under this program are a great stimulus to the business activity of the nation. This money invariably goes into immediate circulation and plays an important part in maintaining our economy, and I believe it is a bulwark against any possible recession in future.
I support wholeheartedly the $40 million being spent on our health program. That program has been in existence for only two years, but already it has accomplished much. It has placed Canada in the lead among the nations of the world in health services. By providing federal funds the government, in co-operation with the provinces, has stimulated research, provided much needed hospital beds, extended mental health care and cancer and tuberculosis control, and launched a war against arthritis and rheumatism, to mention just a few of the accomplishments under this program. We know that already the national health program has paid splendid dividends. Its value will be reflected in future in a decline in illness and disease among Canadians, and in an increase in the production and prosperity of our country. I should like to quote an article which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star a few months ago containing the remarks of an eminent visitor from the United States:
In the provision of public health services, Canada has far outstripped the United States, Dr. Leonard A. Scheele, surgeon-general of the U.S. public health service, told an audience at a Toronto club last night.
Canadian health programs surpassed those in the U.S., he declared, because of effective utilization of research discoveries . . .
In the allocation of federal funds to provide hospital beds, Canada was also far ahead of the U.S., Dr. Scheele declared. The Canadian hospital construction grant program had in a single year allocated federal assistance for the construction of 13,000 additional beds, or nearly one-third of the expected 40,000 to be provided in a five-year period.
For the information of the house I may say that I believe this figure now is closer to
The Budget-Mr. Robertson
25,000	beds, which I think is a remarkable achievement under this program. Then the article goes on:
"At the rate we in the U.S. are going it will take twenty years to provide the necessary hospital space," he added.
So it will be seen that this visitor from the United States, an eminent authority, recognized the great part our national health program is playing in Canadian life. Therefore I say this $40 million we are spending on health services is perhaps the most wisely spent $40 million in our whole budget.
I come next to a discussion of the appropriation for national defence. I note this has been increased to $425 million. It is ironical, I would say, that at a time when we are making every effort to reduce human suffering from disease we are forced, like many other nations, to spend such huge sums on national defence. We are making great strides in the twin arts of taking and saving human life. However, with the situation that exists in the world today, I think there is no alternative. Important as our expenditures on social security may be-and as I said before I take second place to no one in my support of that program-nevertheless I believe that our most important duty as members of this house is to make sure that Canada has an adequate defence. There can be no doubt that if we do not have national security we shall not enjoy any of these social security measures that we prize so much. Therefore I support without question the large expenditure on national defence, and I believe that in the present minister, despite the criticism of the opposition, we have a man well qualified to be in this important post.
Hon. members of the opposition have repeatedly asked the minister for certain secret information with respect to the defence forces of Canada. I believe the minister has been wise and far-sighted in refusing to give this information. As he very well said in a radio address the other evening, what is the use of spending so much money on defence and then telling the Russians exactly what we are doing? Yet that would be the situation if he were to accede to the wishes of the opposition.
I want to take strong exception to some of the remarks which have been made in this house by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). Many times he has implied, if not actually stated, that there are many Liberal members in this house who vote for the government against their convictions. I for one wish to reject that implication in its entirety. I consider it an effrontery to my sincerity, and to the sincerity of other hon.

The Budget-Mr. Robertson members in this house. When we were chosen by the people of our constituencies to represent them in this House of Commons, it showed that they believed in our sincerity. I say again that I reject any suggestion by the leader of the opposition that we are adopting any such course.
In his self-righteous manner, the leader of the opposition has called upon Liberal members to say in parliament what they are saying outside the house. I am ready to accept that challenge. I am ready to tell you what I tell the people of the county of Northumberland. In the first place, I say that in the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) we have a man whose ability, sincerity and humanitarian convictions mark him as one of the most outstanding leaders this country has ever had. I tell them also that I believe the present administration is giving sound government to the people of Canada. We have only to review the prosperity of the years under the Liberal administration to prove that point. I tell them that the social security program that has been developed by the Liberal party is one of the best social security programs to be found in any country in the world. For any further advance in social security, they must look to the Liberal party.
As many hon. members know, the annual meeting of the Progressive Conservative Association of Canada was held in Ottawa not long ago. One of the most remarkable features of this meeting, so far as I can see, was that for the first time there was no suggestion that they should change the name of the party, nor any suggestion that it was about time to call for a new leader. For many years we have been used to that procedure on the part of the Conservative party. I should like to read a quotation from the remarks made by the leader of the opposition as they appear in the Ottawa Journal. In speaking to that meeting, he said:
This is a crusade to return to the people through their elected representatives the control of the business of the country.
We sang, "O Canada, we stand on guard for thee."
Let us organize as this party never organized before so that when another election comes the people of Canada will indeed be able to stand1 on guard for the country they love.
That is the type of material the leader of the opposition gives to his followers.
I should like to quote from an article containing the remarks of a man who spoke at the same meeting, one of the front men in the Conservative party in Canada, Mr. Grattan O'Leary. The article reads:
He said the March budget brought down by finance minister Abbott was nothing more than a documentation of failure, a cry of despair.

"It was a statement to the people that the government did not know what to do and proposes doing nothing," said Mr. O'Leary.
I should like to quote the remarks of another member who spoke at that meeting, the member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins). I ask hon. members to mark this:
"There is an attempt to set up a dictatorship and that is being preached by Prime Minister St. Laurent himself," said Mr. Higgins.
"This Liberal party has been too long in power and its leaders have become arrogant. The situation has become a serious menace to Canada. An alternative party is essential if democracy is to survive in Canada."
That is the type of material that is given to the people of Canada by the responsible members of the Conservative party. When I came to this house last session, I thought the members of the Conservative party had learned something from their experience in the election last June. But when I read such stuff as this I do not wonder that their prospects for getting control of the government in Canada are very slim indeed. To speak of the Prime Minister as did the member for St. John's East is to my mind reprehensible, because if any man represents democracy in Canada it is our present Prime Minister. He is a man who came from humble beginnings, and who rose to a position of great prominence in Canada. He stands high in the regard of all citizens in Canada. Yet a member of this house says that there is an attempt to set up a dictatorship, and that this is being preached by Prime Minister St. Laurent himself. To me such a statement is almost too ridiculous for comment.
We all agree I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that there are difficult times facing all the nations of the world. It was that great American, Franklin D. Roosevelt, who said that to some generations much is given, and of some generations much is expected. I think that we, as Canadians today, must admit we are enjoying the greatest freedom and the greatest privileges that have ever been enjoyed by any generation in any country in the world. I think it is equally true that we, as Canadians, face the greatest responsibility of any generation in Canada. I believe we have even greater responsibility ahead of us, both as individuals and as a nation. In the final analysis, the real strength of any country lies in the feeling of responsibility which exists in the heart and mind of the individual citizen. I say, therefore, that we must brace ourselves for the days ahead, because even in peace the cost will be great. Not only must we complete adequate defences at great cost, but we must also see that even our most humble citizen enjoys the full privileges of citizenship. That must be our answer to

communism, rather than a police state in which every citizen is subject to intolerable suspicion.
Communism will become dangerous only if there are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who feel in their heart they are receiving less than their just due. Should war ever come to us, the cost will be great. It will require all to gain victory; all our wealth, temporarily our freedom, and for many their lives. It will require great moral as well as material rearmament. I believe that in Canada we have the resources, both material and spiritual, to carry us to final victory. There can be no other course. We must continue to give our support to the United Nations. We must continue to lend support to the North Atlantic security pact. We must see that all our citizens enjoy a full life. We must put our faith in divine wisdom. Having done that, if war still overtakes us, then we must face the inevitable threat to our survival with calm determination, skill and courage. We must never buy peace with our freedom and our liberty.

speechtext:
I feel
prompted to take part in this dqbate, Mr. Speaker, not by reason of the budget itself, for it was quite an ordinary budget revealing that the government had no idea in mind as to any changes in financial policy. I am prompted to speak more by reason of what has been said by some of those who have already taken part in the debate. I notice that both in the session of last fall and this session in this parliament there appears to be an attack levelled against our social credit proposals. This attack seems to be carried on by some of the younger or, shall I say, junior members of parliament who have recently come to this house.
To me it is significant that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) himself guards against entangling himself in any arguments with this group with respect to our financial proposals. I think I can say the same thing with respect to his predecessors. The Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley also refused to entangle himself in debate with respect to the monetary proposals which we have made over the years. We can even go back to one of his predecessors and mention the Hon. Charles A. Dunning, who was minister of finance in the Liberal government some years ago when we in this group first made our appearance in the house. He also avoided any entanglement in arguments proposed by us for the revamping and changing of the financial policy of this country. All that finance ministers seem to do with respect to our proposals is not to argue against them but simply to say, "We will not follow your suggestions". If we ask "Why not?" they
The Budget-Mr. Hansell appear to have no answer. As a matter of fact, some of us are becoming a little bit suspicious that some of the older boys in parliament who have met us before in combat have now resorted to the position of chewing the spit wads for some of the younger men to throw.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a dirty trick.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I might say that it seems to be almost habitual that when we come along and make our proposals, which we believe to be sound and which have never been proved to be otherwise than sound, a cry goes up that the country must not dare to have anything to do with our social credit proposals. They do not say why. The cry does not seem to be made in terms of logic. It is simply a cry of danger. Why there should be any danger, nobody appears to know. At this point I think I might read just a few lines from a well-known book written many years ago. The title of it is "Looking Backward" and its author is Edward Bellamy. It was written in fictional style. He transposed himself over the years and then looked backward. In this particular part that I am going to read he assumes that he has been scanning the geography of a certain nation whose lands have been parched but which lands are capable of tremendous productivity. He sees a stream flowing through that land and in his mind he likens the stream to the flow of money. This is the way he puts it:
Let but the famine-stricken nation assume the function it had neglected, and regulate for the common good the course of the life-giving stream, and the earth would bloom like one garden, and none of its children lack any good thing. I described the physical felicity, mental enlightenment, and moral elevation which would then attend the lives of all men. With fervency I spoke of that new world, blessed with plenty, purified by justice and sweetened by brotherly kindness, the world of which I had indeed but dreamed, but which might so easily be made real. But when I had expected now surely the faces around me to light up with emotions akin to mine, they grew ever more dark, angry, and scornful. Instead of enthusiasm, the ladies showed only aversion and dread, while the men interrupted me with shouts of reprobation and contempt. "Madman!" "Pestilent fellow!" "Fanatic! "Enemy of society!" were some of their cries,-
How often have we in this corner of the house, as we have gone through the country, in the early days particularly, been called crackpots. The writer goes on to say:
-and the one who had before taken his eyeglass to me exclaimed, "He says we are to have no more poor. Ha! ha!"
That is a laugh.
"Put the fellow out!" exclaimed the father of my betrothed ... It seemed to me that my heart would burst with the anguish of finding that what was to me so plain and so all important was to them meaningless, and that I was powerless to make it other.

The Budget-Mr. Hansell
That seems to be the picture that is posed for us when we propose how to distribute the abundant production of this land. Our proposals are met with scorn but never are they proved to be false. I must say here that this scorn is not heaped upon us by members like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) nor by men who have studied and who should know. Whether they regard our proposals as feasible and correct or not, I do not know. They do not argue against them. They simply say: "We will not try them." It is some of these other men who suddenly arise and pose as critics that seem to bring scorn down upon our proposals without showing where they are fallible or where they lack logic or common sense. And when they do try to prove we are wrong, they very often prove that they do not know what they are talking about. I might read a little quotation from the London Economist, which is an ultra-conservative paper. It says:
In monetary matters more than In most matters there has been a revolution in the past ten years. But in monetary thought and practice more than in most matters, established habits have in the past been not so much convictions that could be abandoned when circumstances alter, as articles of faith to be carried to the grave.
The hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver), who I believe in general matters is an intelligent man, the other day assumed the role of the critic. I should like to read a passage-

This statement does not silence those critics. May I interject here: Never, never, never have we proposed issuing $9 of additional purchasing power when only $1 additional purchasing power is needed. Yes, that somebody chewed for him to throw, and if he says he chewed the spitball himself, then all he does is to show the measure of his own intelligence. Further down on that page he said:
Money is only goods and services produced.
I do not know with what authority he makes that remark but I should like to have the opportunity to say a word or two about it. Remember, he says, and I repeat: "Money is only goods and services produced". During the depression days we had the experience of banks desiring to collect their debts. Some of the farmers had no money, but they had produced their grain. On one occasion a farmer came in to a banker and he said: "I would like to pay my note, but I have no money. I have plenty of grain." And so one day he drove his truck up to the bank and he began to shovel grain out. He said to the banker: "Here is my money." I do not know if the hon. member for Churchill would have done that, but if production is money why did the banker not take the wheat?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And cancel the loan.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and cancel the loan. They did not do that. They called the police. The man had to shovel the grain back in his truck and take it home to the granary.
What is money anyway? I will read from an authority who I think is perhaps on a level slightly higher than the hon. member for Churchill. I read from Professor Walker who, I believe, is professor of economics at Harvard university. I may have to stand corrected on that. He is a very eminent economist, and in his answer to the question, "What is money?" he says:
Any medium which has reached such a degree of acceptability that no matter what it is made of, and no matter why people want it, no one will refuse it in exchange for his product.
May I quote another authority, whom I think we Will accept, none other than Dr. W. C. Clark, who is the deputy minister of finance. Dr. Clark said:
Money, in the broad sense (now sanctified by popular usage), is any medium of exchange which is generally acceptable in day-to-day business transactions and the settlement of debts and contracts.
I have read that definition which is part of a treatise which Dr. Clark gave before the banking of commerce committee in 1939.
Before going on to another subject in respect to this definition of money may I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to call it six o'clock.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the house rose at six o'clock I was dealing with a rather bold statement made the other day by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver), who said that money is only goods and services produced. I was attempting to give definitions by expert authorities as to just what money really is. Sometimes it is necessary to retrace one's thoughts and go back to the rudimentary principles that were proposed in days gone by.
Quite often when discussing the principles of social credit with those who are perhaps less informed I find that they often turn and say, "Well, I just do not understand social credit." After we get talking with these same gentlemen we are surprised to find that it is not social credit they do not understand, it is the present money system they do not understand. When one talks in terms such as those used by the hon. member for Churchill and says that money is only goods and services produced, he is not talking about social credit money. He is talking about our present system of money. He is talking about Abbott money. Anyone reveals by such a statement that he knows very little of what he is talking about.
Very often we are asked, "Well, now, if you put in social credit, where would you get the money?" Then I turn to my friends and say, "Where do we get money from at the present time?" I find that they do not know. It is not social credit they do not understand, it is the present order of money that they do not understand. When we tell them that the vast amount of our money comes out of the end of a fountain pen they laugh us to scorn. All we have to do is to ask some of the competent authorities where money comes from and they will tell us that after all money is only a system of financial accountancy, merely figures backed by law and applied to prices and other relative matters.
To indicate the intelligence of a good many people, I recall on one occasion asking a medical doctor where money comes from. I even used his own terms and I said, "You are accustomed to the birth of human beings. Tell me how money is born. How does money come into existence? How do we get it? It does not grow on trees. It does not drop down from heaven. How does it come into existence?" I did not expect this medical man to be an expert economist, but he had had several years of university training and
The Budget-Mr. Hansell I think we can assume that a medical practitioner is an intelligent and logically thinking man.
When I asked this doctor where money comes from he said, "Oh, well, I have a field of wheat out here, that is money." I said, "Do you mean that dollar bills grow on the end of the stalks?" He said, "Oh, no, no, I do not mean that." I said, "What do you mean then?" He replied, "I sell my wheat and get money for it." I said, "That does not tell me how money comes into existence," and he responded, "Oh, well, well, well." That was his answer, "Well, well, well." That was the answer of a very intelligent man.
I recall one occasion during the first years of our presence here an hon. member on the other side of the house-he is not here now-made a certain statement. Of course it is known that a member of parliament does not have to have any brains, but usually we expect a man who is intelligent enough to reach this place to have ordinary common sense. A little exchange and play was going on between this hon. member and myself and I asked him on the floor of this house where money came from. Do you know what his answer was? He said, "Why, we earn it."
That was a display of intelligence, was it not? After the house rose I was talking with him out on Sparks street. He was a good friend of mine even though he was a Liberal. I said to him, "How do you account for the fact that one year there is more money in existence than in a previous year? How do you suppose that other money came into existence?" Do you know what his answer was? He said, "Well, I have a mare at home and she casts a foal which is worth $100. In a couple of years that foal grows up to be a very valuable race horse worth $1,000. There is $900 more money in existence." Can you imagine a man of intelligence saying that. I looked at him and said, "Do you mean to say that money increases with the age of a horse?" He did not know what to say. That is the reasoning of some men.

What is the proper way? Is the

speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. Speaker, that is clear, that during a time of credit expansion money is born into existence by the direct action of banks in making loans, and it exists in figures in bankers' books. When anyone goes into a bank to borrow money, he does not borrow the depositors' savings. That is a fact. He goes into a bank; the bank puts a credit entry opposite his name in the form of figures, and when the man walks out of the bank there is that much more money in existence than when he walked in. There is no dispute on that fact; that is the evidence of Mr. Graham Towers, governor of the Bank of Canada.
Let me read some further evidence which seems to me rather striking. These are questions by Mr. McGeer, who was then a member of the house:

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will you tell me why a government with power to create money should give that power away to a private monopoly and then borrow that which parliament can create itself, back at interest, to the point of national bankruptcy?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We realize of course that the
amount which is paid provides part of the operating costs of the banks and some interest on deposits. Now, if parliament wants to change the form of operating the banking system, then certainly that is within the power of parliament.
But never once has the government of this country, since we have been here, attempted to change that banking policy whereby they, themselves, would be able to create the money they need.
I have cited that evidence because I believe it is as well for some of these critics of the Social Credit policy who ask, "where would you get all the money from?" to know where the present government gets this money, and how money at the present time-real, good Abbott money-comes into existence. I am not talking about social credit money. And might I add that Social Crediters would get money from exactly the same place whence it is born into existence today. The one thing we would do would be to see that there was not a shortage of money, and that the power to consume, in terms of money, would be equivalent to the production of the country in terms of prices.

There is just one further point I would like to mention, because it is rather striking. At page 771 of that same banking and commerce evidence Mr. Jaques asked this question:
Would you admit that anything physically possible and desirable can be made financially possible?
To that Mr. Towers answered, "Certainly".
I noticed in the Ottawa Journal the other day an editorial taking Mr. Douglas of Saskatchewan to task because he had made a similar statement. I am not going to take time to read the whole article, because I wish to conclude with a statement in respect to the way we are going to vote. But this editorial in the Ottawa Journal of April 15, written by one of the editors-I do not know who-is captioned "Slogans and Realities" and quotes Premier Douglas as saying, "what is physically possible is financially possible." Whether the quotation is correct or not, I do not know; but we Social Crediters add the word "desirable" so that the statement is, "what is physically possible and desirable can be made financially possible." The editorial takes Mr. Douglas to task for that which they call a slogan, and they say it is not true.
I would ask this question: who is the greater authority, one of the editors of the Ottawa Journal, or Mr. Graham Towers, the governor of the Bank of Canada?
Then, Mr. Speaker, I might also call attention to an advertisement which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of April 5, and I believe in other newspapers throughout this country. It was inserted by the Bank of Toronto. It is very significant that a campaign is now being carried on in Canada to discourage any thinking about monetary reform. And why? Because they recognize that we are approaching the point of underconsumption, which they like to term overproduction, when there will not be enough money to buy the goods we are able to produce. Getting in on the ground floor of argumentation, they are attempting to warn the people not to change monetary policies. This bank advertisement is headed, "What happens to the money you put in the bank?" It goes on:
Business men, large and small, borrow it to expand so that they can serve you more fully and provide a wider range of consumer goods you need.
That statement is an absolute falsehood. I do not know whether the publicity directors of this bank know what they are talking about. Those in charge of publicity do not always know, and are not always expert in the things they have to publicize; but that statement is absolutely false. If those who publicized it knew what they were talking about, then they did it deliberately to deceive
The Budget-Mr. Hansell the people of this country. Banks do not loan the money of their depositors. They create money in the form of loans, which afterwards becomes the money of the depositors.
I wish I had time to read all this advertisement; other parts of it are along the same line.
In the few moments remaining at my disposal I want to state our position with respect to the amendments; it will take only a moment or two. There are two amendments before the house. On April 4 the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) moved an amendment to the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that you do now leave the chair. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) took part in the debate and moved a subamendment. I should like to say something about each of those amendments, and I shall start by considering the one moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party. The first paragraph of that subamendment reads:
This house regrets that the policies of the government. as announced by the Minister of Finance.
(1) indicate that the government is prepared to accept the present level of production as adequate for this country and as placing a limit on the services and security to be provided for our people:
There is no doubt in our minds that the Liberal government is afraid of abundance. For many years they have demonstrated that they have mentalities geared to scarcity. Times without number, almost, we in this Social Credit group have complained against Liberal policies which without question have had the effect of discouraging production. Liberal taxation policies have definitely limited the extent of Canadian production. I go so far as to say, and I do not think anyone can successfully contradict me, that had it not been for the war Canada never would have reached, under Liberal policy, a gross national product of $16,000 million as it did last year. As the consequence of an accident as far as Canada was concerned, but which might have been a deliberately planned war, our people put forth a supreme effort to win the war. Of necessity national production soared to unprecedented heights. We reached a yearly production of $16,000 million of all kinds of goods and services. Now, however, it is clearly evident that the government is as scared as a certain friend of mine who found himself for the first time boosted on the back of a saddle horse. As the horse started to gallop down the road my friend held on to the saddle horn with both hands, fervently wishing that he was safely on the ground again. I am quite sure the government, with their mentality of scarcity, would feel much more at home if Canada's total production were to shrink somewhat below its present

The Budget-Mr. Hansell level. At any rate, no one reading the budget speech carefully can get any other impression than that the Liberals have decided we have reached the limit of their ability to manage an economy. If it gets any bigger it will be beyond them, and someone else will have to take over. They would rather strangle growth than let that happen. Their trade policies; their decided and almost tragic lack of national fuel, steel, sugar, and agriculture policies; their ineptitude in the field of finance: all stand as vocal evidence of the truth of the contention embodied in the first paragraph of the subamendment.
We Social Crediters are apostles of abundance. We sincerely believe there is no good reason why any artificial limit should be placed upon production in Canada. Our production of all kinds of wanted goods and services should be limited only by the extent of our manpower and natural resources. And when we as Social Crediters are entrusted with the management of the people's affairs, the affairs of government, we will stimulate all-out production. What is just as important, or even more so, we will know how to manage a financial policy that will be able to distribute that abundant production equitably to our people so that none will be wasted. For these reasons we find ourselves in complete agreement with clause 1 of the subamendment, and we could vote for it.
Now we come to clause 2, which reads:
(2) make no provision for increased national production through economic planning, public control of investment, public ownership of monopolistic industries, and the full and proper development and use of our resources, so as to ensure a rising standard of living and comprehensive social security for the Canadian people.
I am sure I speak for all my colleagues when I say we are in agreement with the objectives that seem to have been envisaged by the C.C.F. when they drafted this clause of their amendment. Over the years I have noticed that the Social Crediters and the C.C.F., and other groups, have championed the cause of the downtrodden, the underprivileged and the ordinary fellow in the street. I think it is fair to say that both our groups have been fighting for social justice. But, while we seem to be seeking the same objectives in the economic field, there is a very great difference in the methods we would use in trying to reach those objectives.
The C.C.F. subamendment criticizes the government for making no provision for increased national production through economic planning. I think probably that statement is true; but, if I correctly understand the C.C.F. term "economic planning", it is to be done by a planning board whose

powers are set out on page 150 of the book "Make This Your Canada," where I find this-

The task of the commission will be to plan for the production, distribution and exchange of all goods and services necessary to the efficient functioning of the economy: to co-ordinate the activities of the socialized industries; to provide for a satisfactory balance between the producing and consuming power, and to carry on continuous research into all branches of the national economy in order to acquire the detailed information necessary to efficient planning.
My time is almost gone, and I want to add just one statement. To get the full significance of this definition one has to look at examples of the application of the socialistic planning idea. Let us take Britain as an example. In that country they have had a national planning commission consisting of a small group of economists, engineers and statisticians. They have tried to plan the national economy. When the plans were made by this commission they were pretty much in detail. The next step in the process was to see that the plans were enforced; and, though many thousands of people were opposed to the plans, they were forced or compelled to submit to them. In other words the whole basis of the socialistic type of planning is compulsion.
We Social Crediters believe it is necessary that economic planning be done, but most of it should be done by individual enterprise. We have constantly criticized the government for not having given proper leadership in the development of national policies such as fuel policies, production policies of various kinds, transportation policies and so forth. But our idea of planning so far as government is concerned is that it should be a planning of objectives, with leadership being exercised by departments of government or commissions established by the government and responsible to parliament. When it comes to the realization of those objectives that have been planned, Social Crediters have consistently taken the position that inducement ought to be used instead of compulsion. Human beings will do their best under inducement; they will nearly always do less than their best under compulsion. It is because of this fundamental difference in the approach to making and applying economic plans that we cannot support paragraph 2 of the C.C.F. amendment. Our approach to public control of investment, public ownership of monopolistic industries, and the development of our resources is also fundamentally different from that of the C.C.F.

I have another paragraph to read, Mr. Speaker, but I see that you are anxious.
