speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it grieves me greatly to have to hold up the house for a while, but the speech delivered on April 24 by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) requires a certain amount of attention and I intend to give it that amount of attention before we have another vote. This speech will be found on pages 1836 to 1842 of Hansard.
I think it would be a good thing if I were to lay down what I believe are some of the
The Budget-Mr. Blagkmore responsibilities of a member of parliament. I think the people have a right to expect, first of all, that a member of parliament shall either know something of what he talks about, or talk about only those things that he knows something about. When a member of parliament rises on the floor of this house and makes remarks the people all over the country have some right to believe that he is somewhere near right. I think that is a pretty sound principle to lay down.
According to the Parliamentary Guide of 1950, page 265, the hon. member for Churchill was educated at the Royal Military College and obtained a certificate of graduation with honours. He is stated to be a metallurgical engineer. A gentleman with such credentials certainly should be expected to know what he is talking about.
I should like to draw attention to four passages in the speech which he delivered. I shall not read them completely, but will give the first and last words of each passage and later on I shall deal with one or two of the passages in detail. On page 1838 of Hansard we find a passage commencing with the words, "My point" and ending with the words "money is worthless". There is another passage on page 1838 commencing with the words, "This statement" and ending with, "called inflation". There is still another passage on page 1838 commencing with the words, "Money is only goods" and going down to "against these goods". The next passage is on page 1839 commencing with the words, "In the same way" and going down to the words, "lose their value". I do not know to what extent I shall be able to give attention to these passages, but certainly each one needs attention.
May I draw attention to the first one I referred to which is to be found on page 1838 and which reads:
My point is that the Social Credit theorists lead themselves down the garden path by focusing their attention on money and not on production. Without production money is worthless.
Those two statements constitute a complete falsehood with regard to social credit. In the first place we do not know what the hon. member means by theorists, but if the word "theorists" is taken to include Social Credit members of parliament or members of the Alberta legislature or government, then it is completely wrong. The fact that the hon. member uses the word "theorists" will give him a way out in case he needs it. I grant that there are theorists and practical men, and I suppose there are such in the Social Credit movement as there are to be found in plentiful numbers in the Liberal party; but no responsible individual such as a member

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore of parliament at Ottawa or those whom I have mentioned in the Alberta legislature can be included in the statement made by the hon. member.
I challenge the hon. member to produce any passage in Hansard from 1936 to the present time that either proves or even vaguely justifies the statement he made in that passage. The hon. member said:
My point is that the Social Credit theorists lead themselves down the garden path by focusing their attention on money and not on production.
That is absolutely false. Social Crediters base all their thinking and all their talking and all their reasoning on production. They point out that because of the abundance we are able to produce, so much more than the people are able to buy, we have got to the point at which some adjustment has to be made in the purchasing power in the hands of the people so that they will be able to buy the production they are able to produce.
The hon. member can find that idea reiterated dozens of times since 1933. He tells us he went to hear Premier Aberhart in that year. If he did hear Premier Aberhart, and was in Alberta in 1933, then he heard the expression reiterated time and again until the whole province was like a beehive with the expression, "shortage of purchasing power in the hands of the people." And he heard, on the other hand, the bankers and all their supporters saying that we had overproduction. If we have overproduction on the one hand, then certainly we have a surplus of goods. If we have a shortage of purchasing power in the hands of the people we also have a surplus of goods. So that no matter which way the hon. member approaches the problem, his statement is absolutely false and erroneous, entirely. He should know it; and if he does not know it there is something seriously wrong with that member. He threw this false statement on the pages of Hansard before tens of thousands of people from one end of Canada to the other, something which I maintain no member has the right to do.
Let me say to the hon. member that he would have found many, many statements in Hansard giving the truth about social credit if he had taken the time to look for them.
May I refer to the first speech I delivered in the house in 1936, when I first came to parliament. That was my first regular speech in this chamber. Let me read a passage from Hansard for 1936, page 115, and see whether there is any disregard for goods in that speech. I said:
At the same time, what banks can so generously do, and lend the proceeds to the government, and charge them good stiff interest for, I submit that governments ought to be able to find some way or another of doing for themselves.

I am speaking about the creation of money. I continue:
Here is another example. Mr. A. de V. Leigh, secretary of the London chamber of commerce, in a statement reprinted in the Ottawa Citizen on June 8, 1934, makes the following statement:
"The war was paid for as to 30 per cent by actual money belonging to the people-"
Is there anyone who can see any reason why, then, the people of Great Britain should be taxed almost to death to pay for that war, when they already have paid for it?
"-earned by the people; which was invested by the people in war loans;-"
Then note particularly these words:
"-and 70 per cent of the total cost of the war was paid for by the banks very kindly making these book entries, costing them nothing except the ink, paper and the time of the clerk, and lending the result to the nation at interest. The nation owes them money in exchange for their promises-to-pay money which they have not got. Further we have been paying them interest on these promises-to-pay ever since. Interest on war loans amounts to something like five million dollars a day."
Now if the government is going to assert complete freedom for the Dominion of Canada, it is going to take control of such issue. It must be safeguarded, we will grant. It must be managed by men who are responsible and who are trained, men who will honestly and successfully manage that aspect of the nation's life in the interests of the people and not in the interests of any private group.
There is one more thing which must be very carefully considered, and we assume that the Prime Minister has this in mind. Up to the present time the backing for money has been gold. Men have got to the point where they virtually worship the gold standard. It is like a golden calf which they worship to their ruin, but the time must come when we will all realize that the backing of money is not necessarily gold. May I read here a statement by an eminent authority which none will presume to question, the Midland Bank, England, the largest bank in the world? Here is an extract from its monthly review, June-July, 1935.
"In the past four years the progress of ideas has been rapid-the gold value of sterling has dwindled by 40 per cent-neither the government nor the bank does anything about it, and no one is in the slightest degree disturbed, since the pound buys just as much goods and services as in 1931."
In other words, the gold standard has been gradually displaced in England as a backing for goods and services. In our country, with new machinery and scientific knowledge, a high degree of technical skill, and good organization, we can produce an almost infinite amount of goods, and we have hundreds of thousands of men in the country ready to render services; so there ought to be virtually an unlimited backing for what money we wish to produce; at least there should be enough backing to give us the money we need.
That passage alone should have warned the hon. member, if he had taken the time and pains, making him realize that the statement he was about to make was completely wrong. Then I made the following quotation:
"Stability of the value of the pound in terms of goods has replaced stability in terms of gold. At the heart of the matter is a change in the official conception of stability-internal stability is bringing us far greater benefits, in solid economic welfare, than the pursuit of fixity of exchange cpuld

conceivably yield. Clearly this change is nothing short of a revolution-it indicates an almost complete transformation of the monetary system."
And then I went on in my own words:
The social credit group in this parliament believes that the Prime Minister favours the introduction of such a revolutionary change. First, that the dominion government will take control of the issue so as to manage it for the people's welfare; and, second, that little by little in so far as it is necessary they will gradually depart from the gold standard and substitute a goods and services backing, and that such other measures will be taken as will tend to the well-being and increase of the wealth of this country.
While I was not particularly discussing the question raised by the hon. member's statement, nevertheless it is surprising how well I answered him, considering my speech was made over fourteen years before his.
I now wish to read a statement by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). Since we came to the house the hon. member and I have been endeavouring to carry the burden of explaining the views of this group with respect to financial problems; so that whenever we have spoken we have been pretty well expressing the ideas of the group and of the movement. The hon. member for Acadia, speaking on March 3, 1939, had this to say about the $750 million loan, as set out at page 1517 of Hansard tor that year:
Now, we fully realize that there is a well defined limit to the amount of money that can be issued in any period, and so long as it does not go beyond that limit there need not be any fear of inflation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the limit?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The limit is the amount of money necessary to make the great physical demand of the people effective against the production of the country; that is to say, if you have on the one hand goods unsold and on the other hand people requiring those goods, you can give them enough money to buy those goods without any possible danger of inflation.
I believe the hon. member, if he is listening-and I have not had time to notice whether he is or not-will find in that a contradiction of what he has said. He may say, "Oh, I have not had the time to read all the speeches made by members of the Social Credit party." The hon. member has been in this house during one and a half sessions. There have been here ten members of the Social Credit group, any one of whom could have put him right. So there is no excuse, not only for his failing to get correct information regarding Social Credit concepts and policies, but for rising in the house and scattering misinformation throughout the country.
I should like now to quote from speeches delivered since the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) became leader of this group. When he became leader he also became spokesman for the group, spokesman for the
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore Social Credit movement. Speaking on November 7, 1945, as reported at page 2573 of Hansard, he said:
It is different from our present money-I am speaking, of course, of social credit money-but only in this respect, that it is issued into circulation without adding to the nation's debt. And remember that Social Crediters advocate issuing new money only when there are goods and services already in existence to be distributed by money; a dollar of purchasing power for a dollar's worth of goods and services available, no more and no less. I suggest that under such circumstances there could not possibly be any inflation.
Now let me suggest to the government that when unsaleable surpluses of goods begin to pile up on the shelves of the warehouses, as sooner or later they will because of the inherent weakness of the financial system, and when at the same time there are Canadians who need and want these goods for their own use, the government should arrange another credit expansion equal to the value of the goods to be removed, and see to it that this new money finds its way, debt-free, into the hands of consumers, starting first with old age pensioners, the blind, scholars who want to stay in school to finish their education but have not the means to do so, and the unfortunate of the country. I suggest that no Canadian should henceforth ever have to go hungry.

speechtext:
Control over him?

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

speechtext:
Yes; advisory control. At page 3234 of Hansard for 1946 I find these words by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low):
To reassure my hon. friend, let me say that as he learns more about social credit principles he will see that for more than twenty years we have emphasized consistently this fact:	money without
goods is useless. We have also emphasized its necessary accompaniment:	goods without money
is stupid.
That sets it out pretty well. Now I quote from a speech by the same hon. member on May 6, 1947, as it appears at page 2813 of Hansard:
Thoughtful people are asking what there is in the budget to indicate that, as we advance into the period of mass production of consumer goods, the government will have in readiness a policy and machinery to maintain consumer purchasing power at a level sufficiently high to maintain a balanced economy.
At page 2816 of Hansard for the same year, during the same debate the hon. member said:
It is the quantity of money in the pockets to buy that makes employment. Our biggest job in the future will be to maintain that kind of purchasing power at a level high enough to ensure the distribution of our whole production. If we fail in that, our way of life, our freedom, the individual system of responsible enterprise are all doomed.
Again, on page 2817, referring to the Minister of Finance:
I challenge him-and I hope he will listen to what I say to him at this time-to rise in his place in this house and in his rebuttal say what he will do when there begin to appear unsaleable surpluses of goods in our country, the first signs of coming depression.
Again, on December 11, 1947, as recorded at page 187 of Hansard for that year:
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is not a new idea to advocate that the people themselves are the best controllers; certainly it is not a new idea to advocate that the best way in the world to make it >
possible for the people themselves to control prices and the cost of living is for them to have in their hands at all times sufficient purchasing power with which to buy all the goods they have produced if they want them. Our present financial system does not do that. Over a long period our industrial system has resulted in the distribution of less purchasing power than the people needed to buy the goods they produced. That is one of the principal reasons we had to have such things as are being suggested today; that is why we have had to have the most-favoured-nation clauses, and Bretton Woods in trade treaties.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And war.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and war. The simple fact of the matter is that internal pressure to get rid of goods that are in surplus-not surplus above what the people want and can use but surplus above what the people can buy-is one of the greatest causes for the necessity for these bureaucratic or planned controls.
Again on May 21, 1948, at page 4261 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, those words of the hon. leader of the opposition exactly fit the proposals I have made


today, because I have called for the use of tne national credit for family allowances, old age pensions, floor prices, and .so on. Such use of the national credit to the amount of $300 million means that purchasing power to that extent would circulate amongst the people without creating a debt at its source and without accumulating an interest burden throughout its whole life. It need never be cancelled out of existence until that day when production falls short of the purchasing power available in this country.
These passages are unmistakable. Surely if the hon. member had been a little concerned about getting things straight he would have at least consulted the speeches of the hon. member for Peace River. Now I quote from a speech made by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) during the debate in reply to the speech from the throne on March 11, 1949, at page 1404 of Hansard:
In order that a high standard of living may be maintained, we have always advocated that it would be necessary to use a certain amount of national money for the purpose of maintaining the purchasing power of the people at a level sufficiently high to maintain an effective demand against the production of the country. We have never advocated that more money should be issued than was necessary to maintain an effective demand. In other words, we are advocating that national money shall be issued to equate demand with supply.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have always said that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It must be quite obvious that this
is essential if we are to maintain the full development of our resources, because just the minute that demand lags behind supply, industry will reduce production, since no industry can continue to produce unless it can sell.
I should think that would leave no doubt whatever. I think it is a good thing just to show the hon. member that since he has been here in this house there have been statements by Social Crediters in which the whole situation in respect to production and money has been made perfectly clear. May I quote from the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River, following the quotation from Professor Plumptre which the hon. member for Churchill quoted before he proceeded to make his speech at page 1838 of Hansard, to which I have referred. At page 1537 of Hansard for April 4 the hon. member for Peace River said, referring to the expansion of credit:
What for? For the war effort: not to take care of the unemployed, not to offer social security, not to close the gap between the national product and the national income-
Showing once more that before any money whatever would be issued there would have to be production to justify it, and to absorb the money once it was put into circulation.
Now I should like to refer to something I said on the very day the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) spoke. At that time I made a statement which, if the hon. member had been able to be here and listen to it,

would have set him right. In referring to the speech of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), at page 1826 of Hansard I said:
-I would say that it would be a good thing for him to give a little attention to this general question: Canada since 1938 has more than doubled her production. She now is producing by way of $16 billion worth of goods a year; and she expects to be able to produce $16,250 million this year.
Judging by Canadian resources, I find it difficult to believe that we cannot double our production in the next twelve years, as we did in the last twelve. If brilliant young men of the type represented by the hon. member who has just taken his seat would devote their attention to the question of how to turn that full production into well-being of the Canadian people, they would not be cheeseparing, cutting off a little here and a little there. They would really open their eyes as to what could be in the future in a country so abundantly blessed with resources and the ability to transform those resources into the goods and services necessary for mankind.
There was another reference to the rapid increase in production and the possibility that money could be created to distribute that production among the people and enable them to consume it. Then I should like to quote another passage from the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge on October 25, 1949, appearing at page 1118 of Hansard. This is another passage which the hon. member for Churchill certainly could have read.
How much money can be created and used by the state? Enough money can be created and used, spent wisely into circulation, to enable people to buy the surplus goods on the market. If this is done and no more money is issued than enough to enable people to buy the goods, if that money is put into the hands of people who will buy, and is used to consume goods, then there will be no adverse results from the creation and issue of debt-free money.
Certainly that was clear enough; I do not see how words could make it any clearer. The big question is whether the hon. member was trying to find the truth. Now I shall leave that passage I have been discussing and refer for a moment to the statement to which the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) alluded, the second one I referred to a while ago. I quote from page 1838 of Hansard: This statement does not silence those critics. The creation of money as advocated by the hon. member can be done, but it is only another form of hidden taxation, and the most extreme and insidious form of all. Let us assume that we have $10 worth of production, and that there is $9 of purchasing power available.
Then assume that the government listens to our Social Credit friends and creates an additional $9 of purchasing power. We now have $18 of purchasing power and still only $10 worth of goods to back it up. By this indirect method the government will have taken in taxation half the goods. This type of hidden taxation has been used by unscrupulous governments many times in history; it is called inflation.
Once more the member implies, if he does not completely assert, that, in a case where there was $10 worth of production and only 55946-125
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore $9 worth of purchasing power, Social Credit-ers would advocate the creation of $9 of extra purchasing power. This is absolutely fallacious as the statements I have just read indicate. Would it not have been much better if he had said that, the government having $10 worth of production and $9 worth of purchasing power, it created $1 worth of purchasing power? How different it would have been in that case. The $9 worth of purchasing power would have been supplemented by the creation of $1 worth of extra purchasing power, so that you would have then had $10 worth of production and $10 worth of purchasing power. It would have balanced the economy; the surplus would have been distributed and prices maintained. Why any member would stand up and misrepresent the position of any other group when that position is scientifically stated, as the position of this group has been, it is utterly beyond me to comprehend. I wonder if someone else wrote the speech for him.
If the hon. member was in Alberta at the time he says he was, he heard Premier Aberhart in the days when he was campaigning. I do not see how he could very well have avoided hearing about certain books. One of those books was "Unemployment or War", by Maurice Colbourne; one was "This Age of Plenty"; and another one was "Distribute or Destroy". Those three books very adequately and clearly set forth the surplus production which has resulted from the widespread use of machines and technological skills, and the consequent shortage of purchasing power which has resulted in overproduction or underconsumption. There can be no possible excuse for a man who wanted to find the truth failing to get one or other of those books and read it.
People will say, it is a little bit strange that you should name those books. It is not strange at all. The thing that taught Premier Aberhart the truth concerning social credit and the unbalance between production and consumption in our day was "Unemployment or War" by Maurice Colbourne. I remember clearly the time when Premier Aberhart first got a copy of the book. I remember he read it over four times before he would leave it. When he first got it he sat up all night reading it. It gave him a new idea. It showed him how production increases so rapidly that surplus production develops and the only way in the world whereby purchasing power balances production is to have a war or to destroy a whole lot of production. As we have seen in the last two wars production is destroyed and purchasing power is increased in such a way that we have prosperity during the war. The Social Credit stand has been

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore that we certainly do not have to have a war in order to increase purchasing power in relation to the goods. We have found a means whereby we can do that without a war a means that will make everybody well off.
This gentleman I think should read the book "This Age of Plenty", written by C. Marshall Hattersley. The book is written in a scholarly manner that would be appreciated by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver). The book "Distribute or Destroy" is very clear; the title conveys the meaning that has been developed in the book.
It will be wondered by some whether what I have said about the stand which this group takes conforms with the stand of the social credit secretariat in London. Social Credi-ters throughout the world, when they are well informed, are more or less in close touch with the social credit secretariat in London, generally speaking, as to the philosophy and teaching. I have in my hand a book entitled "Elements of Social Credit", which was published in 1946 under the direction of the social credit secretariat of London, of which the advisory chairman is Major C. H. Douglas. He was the originator of the social credit idea, and from him we have all gathered our inspiration. What this textbook says then is fairly authentic concerning social credit-in fact, I will say it is absolutely authentic. I should like to read several passages from the book, but they will be couched in the careful language of Major Douglas, will be rather scientific and not very clear. If anyone will study them, however, the meaning will become quite clear. It is not observable on first reading.
I quote now from page 4:
The course, then-
That is the course on social credit making up the book.
-aims at as complete instruction as possible in a limited number of matters concerning social credit. All the matters which concern social credit have not yet been investigated. It is the youngest of studies, though possibly the most vitally important.
Notice these words.
It concerns the efficiency of human beings in association (or in society) as measured in terms of human satisfaction.
And now put in the ordinary language of the man in the street, that simply means that social credit means the production power of a group of people working in a community with their resources to produce goods and services and deliver them as, when and where required; that is the meaning of social credit. The social credit movement is a


movement based on the philosophy or technique in virtue of which it becomes possible for the community to gain access to its social credit and use it.
Now, I wish to read two or three other small excerpts from this book. I shall read now from page 7. There social credit is defined as:
. . . the efficiency, measured in terms of human satisfaction, of human beings in association (or in society).
This passage has the same meaning as the other passage I quoted. Again on the same page, we find this:
The power of human beings in association to produce the result intended, measured in terms of their satisfaction.
Of course this means the power of the community to produce goods. The attention of the reader is concentrated upon goods and services.
On page 8 of this book we have the following quotation:
Social Credit, then, is a fact, not a theory. We shall try in this course to get to know as much as possible about this power-about every means of increasing it and every means of diminishing it.
The power referred to there is the power to produce goods with the resources the community has.
The result will be more power in our hands to control it, whether we use that power or not.
On page 25, I read the following:
The speculations concerning such matters have nothing to do with us as Social Crediters, unless they can be shown to affect the power of society to produce the result intended as measured in terms of human satisfaction.
Once again, that means goods.
It is the definition of social credit that limits our technique.
There is one more quotation I should like to read from page 41:
. . . the efficiency of human society as measured in terms of satisfaction to individuals (for all of those who support human society, or participate in human association, are individuals).
Now, the quotation as I have given it there once more refers to goods, so that the whole social credit attitude is based on the goods supply which is available and which may be rendered available with the means of production at the disposal of the community and the resources which are there to be worked up into goods and services beneficial and desirable to the community.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that from this time forward all the members of the House of Commons, of any party whatever, will at least take the pains to know just exactly what social credit stands for. We are going to endeavour to understand the things for which

the other parties stand. We shall never advance this country by misrepresenting each other's stand.
If the Liberals cannot discredit social credit by placing the true meaning of social credit before the people and attacking it, that is clear evidence that social credit must have a far better case than they would have us believe.	Surely if	the case against	socialcredit is	strong, all	that	is necessary	is totell the truth about it. There is a group of people right here in the house who are able to show	the truth	and	to establish	it toanybody's satisfaction here in the house, to any degree that is desired. All we ask is the privilege	of letting	the	people understand
what social credit is, so that, when they talk, the people in the country can find out what it is. If social credit is sound, everybody wants to know; and I am sure even the Liberals want to know if it is sound. If it is unsound, everybody wants to know, and Social Crediters want to know.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that it will not be necessary for me to make another speech like this as long as I am in parliament.

I promise, Mr. Speaker, that I will not detain the house for more than two or three minutes from this vote that is to be taken. My kind and learned friend the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has supplied me tonight with the perfect example of the kind of dollar that we do not want in Canada, this one which I am holding in my hand. Unfortunately, however, it is exactly the kind of dollar that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is using today, and I am going to demonstrate that it is. Furthermore, I will not expect the minister to refute this in his rebuttal; but when his estimates come up, I want him to be prepared to meet what I am going to tell him now and to explain whether I am right or wrong.
If anyone will just take the trouble to examine an authentic work by Professor James Holladay called "The Canadian Banking System", which was written not too long ago and which now reposes in the parliamentary library, he will find that it is a book in which there is a foreword written by C. M. Short, an economist for one of the chartered banking companies in Canada. In his foreword Mr. Short writes an unqualified endorsement of what Dr. Holladay said. On pages 150 and 151 of the book Dr. Holladay shows the kind of money that Canadians are dealing in today as a result of the money system that they have adopted under the various finance acts and banking acts. This is what he says: "Under the present banking 55946-1251
The Budget-Mr. Low
system in Canada, one dollar of basic gold deposit can be expanded and stretched into $84 worth of purchasing power". That is the kind of stretch there is, 84 times, in the kind of dollar you are using. Whenever anybody starts talking about rubber money and Social Credit funny money, I will challenge him to produce a funny money to compare with what you are using.
Furthermore, it is not just the question of stretch that causes the difficulty. When the stretch takes place, it must be remembered that unless something is done to ease the tension, the stuff will fly back and knock your head off. That is exactly what happens when the banking system begins to call in the expansion of credit that they have made in the course of stretching one dollar of basic gold deposit into $84 of purchasing power. It is deflation that is the real danger. What we are trying to get away from is the amount of stretch followed by the amount of retraction. Social credit money would not do that. Social credit money would not allow of an unprecedented expansion or stretch of that kind followed by some type of deflationary contraction. Social credit money would be based upon a 100 per cent cash reserve system, and therefore would be without that stretch.
I just point out to you the fact that in the last year before the war the total amount of gold, currency and bank deposits in Canada was approximately $2,248 million. What is it today, in 1950?. It is three times as large. Where did it come from? It came from the amount of stretch, which the hon. member for Temiscouata has demonstrated so kindly by bringing in this rubber dollar that I hold in my hand, stretch through the banking system, as a result of expanding credits. As I have pointed out time and again, the danger is that at some time or other the banks may begin to lose confidence in borrowers' ability to repay and, when they do, start calling in loans which represent expansion. Then they will contract the credits and leave quantities of goods unsold or unmovable. Social credit says that that is not the state of things that should prevail in Canada.
I thank the hon. member for Temiscouata for bringing in this rubber dollar, because it demonstrates exactly what I wanted to put over, namely that the kind of dollar being used today by the Liberal government is a rubber dollar that has been stretched 84 times.

Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act and to provide, amongst other things:
1.	That the excise tax of five per cent on toilet soap be repealed effective on and after March 29, 1950.
Resolution agreed to.
2.	That the sales tax on the following articles be repealed effective on and after March 29, 1950-
ice cream: drinks prepared from fresh milk; prepared whipping cream.
Would this also include prepared drinks made out of milk such as Oval-tine and chocolate malted milk?
As far as the trade-named article is concerned, the answer is "No." As far as the second article is concerned, the answer would be "Yes", if it is prepared from fresh whole milk.
There would be as much or perhaps more prepared milk in the Ovaltine than in the chocolate malted. I refer to the chocolate malted milk that is prepared and sold in the can.

I am not an expert on this sort of milk, but my recollection is that chocolate malted milk is sold as such as a preparation whereas Ovaltine is put out in a prepared form with which milk is mixed afterward. Milk itself is sales tax free, anyway.
Whole milk.
Fresh milk.
Chocolate drinks are made of skim milk.
I should have said fresh milk.

These prepared drinks in the containers are at least half made out of milk. Half of the contents is milk. They contain milk, eggs, and things of that kind. Why is that not included here?
Excise Tax Act Amendment

The answer is the same as I gave before. Somewhere there has to be a dividing line, and the dividing line requested last year by many members on this side of the house and on the other side was an exemption for dairy products such as ice cream and drinks made out of fresh milk. That has now been granted. It has not yet been considered proper to give such an exemption to these very special prepared drinks. The intent here of course is to assist the dairy industry. That can be best done by the adoption of this motion.
I wish to ask another question. We have here a reference to prepared whipping cream. Does that refer to the new gadget now on sale, in the plastic container?

It includes more than that. Actually most whipping creams have some ingredients in them to make them whip more easily. It includes that type, and this new one which has the carbonic acid gas in it, so that when the cream comes out it is already whipped.
It includes that?
Yes.

You said first that whipping creams have something in them. I do not think the pure food regulations would allow anything like that. I am referring to these prepared whipping creams in the plastic container. Are not those containers manufactured in the United States? Are they manufactured here in Canada?
I am afraid I have not the least idea.

If they are manufactured in the United States-I understand it is an American product-I do not think this should apply to them at all. The cream would be all right, but it has all kinds of mixtures in it.

Getting back to the purpose of the resolution: it is to give aid to the dairy industry. No matter whether the containers are made in Canada or in the United States, the cream in those containers is Canadian cream.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I am glad to have that admission from the parliamentary assistant, that the list would be a list as thick as Hansard. Does he mean as thick as Hansard of March 28 or of yesterday? In that connection may I point out that at page 30 in the budget papers appended to Hansard of March 28 the Minister of Finance has indicated that of the total revenues of the federal government last year 49-8 per cent were derived from direct taxation and 39-9 per cent from indirect taxation, the remainder of 10-3 per cent being attributable to non-tax revenue and special receipts and credits.

It seems to me if we are going to get away from these indirect taxes, which do not bear any relationship to ability to pay, that a very good place to begin would be by way of a further elimination of the sales tax.
Since the parliamentary assistant feels it is not wise to put on Hansard a volume as thick as Hansard, may I ask him if he has any information concerning the percentage of purchases made by Canadian people that have the sales tax applied to them?

That would be difficult to obtain. When I referred to a list as thick as Hansard, I would say to the hon. member that he need only step into a jewelry shop, look around him and see all those articles

displayed, every one of which has a sales tax on it, to realize why the exact description of these articles would fill many pages. On the other hand, to give at least the headings in schedule III, might I point out that almost all foodstuffs are exempt, almost all things used in farming, mining and quarrying operations, and equipment for marine and fisheries are exempt, and things connected with religious, charitable and educational activities. A very large list of building materials is exempt.

I think so.

The parliamentary assistant has mentioned exemptions in respect of educational equipment. I am thinking particularly of books. I do know that books on the curricula of recognized universities and schools are exempt from sales tax. I also believe that that sales tax, however, is applied to reference books which professors in universities and teachers in educational institutions require for reference either in connection with work in the curricula or for the improvement of their own standard of education.
This seriously affects professors and teachers who in view of their qualifications, as a class, are not particularly well paid, as compared with people in business, or other vocations. I believe we need more rather than less books. For example the number of books per capita read in Canada compares very unfavourably with the record in other countries, notably Great Britain. It should be the policy of the government to encourage rather than to discourage the reading of books by such a device as placing taxes upon them. I am referring to books of an educational nature entering the country. This should be brought forcibly to the attention of the government. I know it has been asked for in the past, but I do not know to what extent the government has given it consideration.

I agree with the hon. member that it is an important matter, and it is a point which has been discussed at some length. I might point out, to begin with, that a very great range of books today are free from sales tax and, if they are imported, from customs tariff. They include:
Books which are included in the curriculum of any university, college or school in Canada for use as textbooks or as works of reference, not to include dictionaries; printed books, pamphlets and cards for use in schools to test the degree of intelligence of pupils; all books for bona fide libraries, and being the property of the organized authorities of such libraries and not in any case the property of individuals or business concerns, under such regulations as may be prescribed by the minister; directories for free reference libraries; books received from free lending libraries abroad, subject to return under customs supervision within sixty days.
The great difficulty with the class of books to which the hon. member refers, those in private possession, is to draw the line between what are educational books and what are not. It is a very difficult line to draw, a line which also greatly affects these gentlemen in the taxation division, because obviously they have to keep abreast by buying these very expensive books. At the moment the best division that can be devised as far as tax purposes are concerned is the one I have just read.

I trust the question I am going to ask will not be considered trivial, because I am interested in the welfare of the boys and girls of the country. I should like to know the minister's answer when I ask him how the repeal of the excise tax on ice cream and drinks prepared from fresh milk is passed on to the consumer. The boys and girls still buy ice cream cones that are scooped out of the freezer with the same scoops, and are just as small as ever. They pay the same prices as before. Drinks prepared from fresh milk are still poured into the same size tumblers we have always used, and we still have to pay the same price. It is an admirable thing to repeal the excise tax on these articles, and I am not disappointed with that; but so often these tax reductions or removals are not passed on to benefit the consumer. I should like to know how the repeal of that tax is passed on to the benefit of the consumer. I do not know why this budget should not go down in history as the government's ice cream budget. On the whole it has been cold comfort to most people. When the youngsters cannot get any more ice cream for their money than they got in the past, or a larger drink of malted milk than in the past, certainly it is cold comfort to them, though I do not suppose the boys and girls know very much about budgets.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I am forcibly reminded of the debate in this connection last year. At that time the hon. member for Melfort, who is sitting right in front of the hon. gentleman, raised the same point. I told him then our calculation showed that the saving would be about one-sixth of a cent on an ice cream cone and one cent on a brick. As I recall it, the response to that observation, particularly by members coming from Quebec ridings, was that that was all right, because it would be the primary producer who would pick up that extra saving. Obviously it is impossible for the retailer to pass on a saving of one-sixth of a cent, but it does make his ice cream a little more attractive to sell in competition with other goods a child might normally buy with his five cent piece. As far as the saving on ice cream bricks is concerned, I believe in some localities the saving of one cent has been passed on. Once again, however, I do not think the intent here was to aid either the child or the retailer. The plea I heard last year was for aid to the dairy farmer, who had been hard hit by the sale of margarine.

One other way would be to fix a standard for ice cream, and say that the ice cream could be somewhat enriched. It seems to me the ice cream we have been
Excise Tax Act Amendment getting for the last several years has been made very largely with powdered milk, and with very little cream in it. If they put a little more cream in their ice cream I think it would help a great deal.
I shall draw my hon. friend's remarks to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture.

Last session I asked the Minister of Agriculture if the cream content of ice cream could not be raised, and shortly afterward I was informed that it could be, and it was raised from 10 per cent to 13 per cent.
Thank you.
Does the retention of the sales tax on schoolbooks also apply to all school equipment?
No, it does not apply to all school equipment.
What is the situation regarding school busses? I believe the excise tax was taken off last year, but does the sales tax still apply?
The excise tax was taken off; the sales tax still applies.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Has the parliamentary assistant the answer to the question I asked a moment ago? What about clothing?
There is a sales tax on clothing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Then I have just this further comment on this resolution. We are all glad to see the sales tax taken off some items, but our point is that it should be taken off still more. I refer once more to the table I have already indicated, on page 1306 of the budget papers which were appended to Hansard for March 28. That table shows not only the larger brackets I gave a few moments ago, but also in more specific detail that excise taxes, in the whole of the last fiscal year, accounted for 22-3 per cent of the revenue of the federal government. That heading of excise taxes would include some taxes other than the sales tax, but I think I am correct in saying that the sales tax is the major item. On the other hand the percentage of the total raised by individual income taxes was only 24 per cent; in other words they are about the same. Canadians were led to feel that something generous was done for them when the income tax was lowered in 1949, but I think most Canadians will realize the significance of the percentages I have just mentioned. These show that taking Canadians as a whole, for every dollar we pay in income tax, and know we are paying, we pay a dollar in excise tax that we do not know about.

Excise Tax Act Amendment
The most undesirable feature about the dollar we pay and do not know about is that it is assessed against Canadians without any necessary relationship to ability to pay. Amounts collected under the income tax are related to some extent to the ability of the taxpayer to pay, but these excise and sales taxes are the same whether the purchaser is living on an old age pension, or a superannuated civil servant's pension, or a veteran's or disability pension, or a war veteran's allowance, or is a worker at $150 or $200 a month, or is a person in the higher income brackets. In other words I am pleading with the government again, in assessing the whole financial situation with respect to federal revenues, to get away from the indirect taxes that are not based upon ability to pay, and move in the direction of a fairer kind of taxation.

I only wish I had at hand the very excellent reference to Hugh Dalton which I gave last year, about the place of indirect taxation in any practical taxation field. It is quite true that theoretically the income tax is the fairest tax, being based on ability to pay; but every country that in time of war has imposed excessive rates of income tax has found they have had a very bad effect on the production of individuals, groups of individuals and companies. Somewhere there must be a balance, that is a balance between what we obtain from direct taxation and indirect taxation. In this country we have tried to make our indirect taxation progressive, as is the income tax. In the case of the income tax, the higher your income the higher the tax.
With our indirect taxation, first of all there are the lists, which you willsee in Hansard tomorrow, of the goods on which there is no sales tax or excise tax. It will be found that the person to whom the hon. member referred, the person on old age pension or burnt-out pension, would obtain a great part of his actual requirements from the goods in that list. Then there is the other group, containing practically everything else in the country, on which sales tax is levied. It is quite true that one of the items there is clothing, but once again there is the matter of progression. The purchases of clothing by persons in those circumstances will be far less than those of persons with higher incomes.
Then there is. the third group in our taxation structure of less essential goods on which a further ten per cent is levied. This covers luxury goods such as perfumes, leather goods and things like that. Once again one does not expect the people on these small pensions to purchase many of these articles.
Lastly, we have the excise duties which are traditionally high on liquor and tobacco.


It is quite true that many of these people do derive great comfort from tobacco. On the other hand, so far as the liquor tax is concerned, you will *not find very many purchases being made by the people in these low income groups. On the other hand, the people in the higher income groups do spend an increasing part of that income on goods upon which there is a heavier tax. We have tried, therefore, even with our indirect taxes, to have a measure of progression so that the higher a man's income the more he is likely to have to pay in such taxes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I just ask the parliamentary assistant to confirm or deny this comment? An impression might be obtained from what he has just said that a fairly large proportion of these excise taxes might be taxes on liquor and so on. As I read the table the Minister of Finance gave on page 1213, it seems to me to be clear that the sales tax accounted for $400 million in the last fiscal year, and that the other excise taxes-which I take it are the liquor taxes-accounted for only $153 million. If I am wrong, will the parliamentary assistant correct me?

The fourth level is the group with no sales tax. The first group is with the sales tax, then the group with excise tax, the group with ten per cent, and then there is this top group, including liquor and tobacco, on which there is an excise tax at a very high rate. Last year we raised from them $229,190,669, and from the sales tax, we received-perhaps it would be easier to put it in round figures-$415 million; and liquor and tobacco taxes, $229 million.

Mr. Chairman, during our discussion on the sales tax last fall, I had occasion to make a rather strong plea for the remission of sales tax on machinery purchased by municipalities. As I pointed out on that occasion, that arrangement does exist under which the moneys paid in this way are remitted to the provincial governments. I suggested that the government might extend this same consideration to municipal governments. A partial explanation was given on that occasion, but I believe it was said that further consideration would be given to this matter.
Obviously, if consideration was given it had no particular bearing upon the attitude of the government because no concessions have been made in that direction. In my plea last fall I was supported by members from other parties within the house, in fact by members who had a good deal of municipal experience and who sit on the government benches. The association of rural municipalities in my own province unanimously

endorsed a resolution asking for favourable consideration of this matter. I rather fancy that the same action has been taken by municipal governments through their organizations in other provinces. No doubt the government has received representations in this respect, and I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant if he can give some justification for the decision which the government still persists in adopting in this connection.

Representations have been received within the last year from the municipalities in every province in Canada on this matter, I believe. Naturally every group who have a tax of any description, whether it be income tax, sales tax or excise tax which applies to them, are always keen to see that tax removed.
But this is a government.

Yes. and through their
endeavours consideration was given to the request, as it is always given to a request for the removal of a tax; but the budget committee decided, and the government approved, that because of our need for revenue we could not at this time remove the sales tax on that equipment.

Do you
ever have anyone asking to be taxed?
We did in one instance.

There are machines purchased by municipalities upon which no tax should be applied, and that is fire-fighting equipment. We read of the tragedies which happen in this country in which people lose their lives because the municipality in question was unable, through economic circumstances, to buy the proper fire equipment. We read continually of the poor type of engines, and some places go without fire equipment at all because of the high cost of that machinery. I do not see how any government can ju'tify the imposition of a tax on machines used for the preservation of life. The Minister of National Defence quite freelj admitted to me in the course of debate in this house that these machines form part of the defence equipment of this country. Municipality after municipality is in the position of having either inadequate fire equipment or none at all. I should like to hear a comment from the parliamentary assistant on the justification of the present tax against such fire equipment. Has he anything to advance?

I cannot add anything to the answer I have just given.

In connection with the taxes on macninery owned or purchased by municipalities, will the parliamentary assistant say whether the provincial governments in every province of the dominion pay these taxes?
The answer is no.

May I ask the parliamentary assistant about another type of equipment, and the reason why some consideration has not been, or may not be, given to it? The parliamentary assistant may be aware of a resolution passed by the Canadian construction association at its annual meeting in Montreal last January. I should like to bring it to his attention. It reads as follows:
Whereas:	The incidence of the federal sales tax
of eight per cent falls inequitably on many types of building and road construction material, some being exempt and others, without apparent logical reason, continuing subject to the impost.
And whereas: The previous action of the government in removing the sales tax from certain construction materials was of great value in reducing construction costs.
Therefore be it resolved: That this association petition the Hen. Minister of Finance to further reduce construction costs and to remove the present uneven incidence of sales tax on building and engineering materials by extending the exemption from such tax to all building and engineering materials.
And further: That similar representations be made to all provincial and municipal governments which impose similar taxes on building and engineering materials.
May I ask the parliamentary assistant whether any consideration has been given to the removal of sales tax on that type of equipment?

A great deal of consideration has been given in the last three years to the exemption of building materials. The exempted list has been continually revised and today it covers almost every item used in the construction of the ordinary house. When you get into the more elaborate type of construction, such as theatre construction and the fancy types, some of the fittings used there are subject to sales tax. Once again it gets back to this idea of getting some measure of progression into our sales tax. We have been reviewing that list with regard to building materials, and I believe we have exempted most of the things that go into the construction of the ordinary home. If you look, you will find that almost every possible thing which is used in the construction of the ordinary home is being exempted from sales tax.

I should like to refer to the case which occurs along the border where a United States firm may come in and bid on a contract for road work, digging a pipe line

Excise Tax Act Amendment or on other contracts which may be let in Canada. They bring their equipment in from the United States to do that work. As to the Canadian company obtaining their equipment, with the sales tax and tariff it costs them approximately 35 per cent to 40 per cent more than the equipment costs the United States company bidding on the same contract. What is the position of that equipment being brought in here? Is there any charge or tariff against it? If not, there is some most unfair competition in the contract being bid on.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Before the parliamentary assistant replies to this question, there is something I should like to draw to the attention of the committee. I should have interfered before. speechtext: Order. Since the discussion has been proceeding on paragraph 3, shall we consider paragraph 2 as having been allowed to stand? Will the parliamentary assistant explain what articles are referred to in
[Mr. Wright. 1

paragraph 3? Does that mean that articles of every kind and character bought by an institution are exempt from sales tax, including hardware, clothes and furniture for the use of the insiitution?

That is the intention. There has always been a strong feeling that this exemption which was granted to the hospitals should be extended to a group of institutions which are closely allied to hospitals. For example, in my province, and I am quite sure in other provinces also, there are the homes for incurables which are not properly hospitals. But nevertheless they require, for the treatment of these old people, a great deal of hospital equipment such as hospital beds; in addition, they supply medical equipment which would be supplied free if these incurables, instead of being in a home for incurables, were in a proper hospital. As you know, one of the great attempts being made today is to try to clear our hospitals of that type of case and put old people in old people's homes or nursing homes. That is one of the reasons.
The second class to which this section applies is orphanages. It seemed unfair that this sales tax exemption should be given to all hospitals and not to orphanages. There are some hospitals which are in not too bad financial condition whereas no one knows of any orphanage which is in a good financial position. So this resolution, which has been demanded again and again by members in all parts of the house, has been brought forward. It is going to be necessary when the bill is brought down to spell out clearly just what type of institutions are going to be covered so that there will not be any abuse. We have had to do that in connection with the hospitals too. With the hospitals we take the certification of the provincial government as evidence that they are bona fide hospitals. But the group of institutions which are covered in this resolution will be carefully enumerated when the actual bill is brought down, and goods bought by those institutions for use in those institutions will be free from sales tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall paragraph 3 carry?

No. There is one point I am not quite clear on. I think this is a first-class amendment. Suppose one of these institutions goes to a retailer or to a wholesaler to buy certain merchandise. How do they get that eight per cent sales tax back?
Provision will be made in the act for refund of the sales tax which was paid.
Who will refund the money, the retailer or wholesaler?
It will go to the institution. The institution itself will file, as do hospitals today, for refund on those things which were bought.
Is that on anything they buy, no matter how small it may be?
No matter how small or large.

Reading this paragraph, I notice it contains the words "public institution". Is there any provision to exempt private hospitals from the payment of sales tax on similar materials or articles purchased?

The distinction is that a private hospital that has been run for gain or profit has never qualified for this. They had to be public institutions which take in the general public and were supported by grants from the public treasury, provincial, municipal or federal.
Perhaps it is run for profit but makes a loss.
Like the one in Montreal; Notre Dame, I think it is. It is nearly bankrupt.

Articles and materials for the use of any public hospital certified as such by the Department of National Health and Welfare, when purchased in good faith for the exclusive use of such hospital and not for resale, are exempt.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the paragraph carry?

No. I would suggest that the government should give consideration to a revision of that section to enable private institutions which are really being operated for charity, such as those institutions or hospitals which are conducted by the Sisters, to get this advantage.
Those are covered in this, as are the hospitals.
They could be certified.
But they are private institutions, are they not?

They are not private institutions in the sense that they are run for gain or profit. Such hospitals have been covered in this previous section and it is the intention to cover in the bill such religious hospitals, orphanages or old people's homes. In the bill it will be necessary to spell out carefully exactly the type of public institution to which we are going to give this aid. We
Excise Tax Act Amendment do not intend this aid to be given to old people's homes which are run for profit or hospitals which are run for profit.
Old people's homes that are run by a municipality will be included?
If they receive grants from the provincial government by way of assistance, that qualifies them.

I for one support paragraph 3 in its reference to these institutions and the exemption from sales tax. I notice it refers to the aged, infirm or incapacitated persons. This brings to my mind an important matter which I have brought to the attention of this committee upon previous occasions. We have in Canada, for example, an organization known as the Red Cross which solicits funds and does excellent work for the unfortunate in cases of flood, fire, disaster and so on. After working hard to procure the money, from which it gets no personal benefit since it is used for the assistance of the unfortunate, the government jumps into the picture and grabs sales tax on many of the commodities which it purchases and gives to the unfortunate. I have often wondered what justification there could be for the government grabbing this slice.

The slice to which my hon. friend refers could best be referred to as a crumb. All items used in Red Cross hospitals are exempt, just as are those in any other hospital. Most of the aid given by the Red Cross, as I recall it, is in the nature of food, and food is exempt from sales tax, or medical equipment; and you will find that most medical equipment is also sales tax free.

It is all a question of whether you kick a man hard or not so hard. There is a principle involved. While I appreciate the fact that many things are exempt, it is true that certain things still bear that sales tax. It was a matter of principle, not so much a matter of dollars. If there is such a small amount of money involved, there should be all the more reason for the government cutting the sales tax out there, because a moment ago the parliamentary assistant emphasized the necessity for procuring revenue as his reason for the government not giving favourable consideration to the other matters which I brought up a few moments ago. This was just a matter of principle.
The matter of principle goes a little beyond the Red Cross. There are many good charities in this country; there are some doubtful charities.
I suppose so.

The thing is, any act applied to charities would have to indicate very care-

Excise Tax Act Amendment fully the qualifications of the charity, and that is a very difficult thing to do. It is much easier, as far as administration is concerned, to see that the principal thing is handled by the Red Cross, and all things handled by Red Cross hospitals are sales tax exempt.
There are many old folks homes that may be operated for gain. How will this repeal apply to the Salvation Army, which operates old folks' homes?

The Salvation Army today have their hospitals classed as public institutions and if they run their old folks' homes -and I am sure they do-in the same fashion, they will get it. The type of old folks' homes which will not be exempt are fairly common on Vancouver island. They are places to which people who have some means actually go and pay for their care. People live together in a small community in pleasant cottages, and these cottages are classed as old folks' homes. They are not in the same category as hospitals run by the Salvation Army or by a municipality or a province.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I should like to know if institutions which at present can pass these other requirements and receive aid from institutions like the Red Feather will qualify?
I would ask the hon. member to wait until he sees what is actually in the bill. Let us not discuss it in too much detail just now.

Before the resolution carries I want the parliamentary assistant to answer the question I raised with regard to United States contractors coming into Canada with equipment and bidding on contracts against Canadian contractors who have to pay sales tax, excise tax and customs duties on their equipment.

I would ask the hon. member to hold that question until the third group of resolutions on the customs tariff are up. It is a very interesting question. I myself would like to have the answer to that. If the hon. member will ask the question when the third set of resolutions on the customs tariff are up I shall have the answer then.
Resolution 3 agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
We will now revert to resolution 2.
2. That the sales tax on the following articles be repealed effective on and after March 29, 1950-ice cream, drinks prepared from fresh milk; prepared whipping cream.

This resolution proposes the removal of the sales tax on ice cream, drinks prepared from fresh milk, and prepared whipping cream. I wish to make one or two brief


observations. These foods that are enumerated here fall within the category, generally speaking, of prepared foods; but there are a number of prepared foods that are still subject to sales tax. One can certainly approve the proposal to remove the sales tax on these three, but one wonders at the same time why the government should stop there. In the case of prepared foods that are essential, why should not the removal be extended to them? We are now faced with the situation where the cost of living is the highest in the country's history.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the hon. member propose to make a proposal modifying this resolution? If he is not prepared to do so I would say he is not in order unless he speaks on ice cream, drinks prepared from fresh milk, and prepared whipping cream.

I am speaking on the subject of prepared foods, of which these are three examples selected by the government. In his budget speech the Minister of Finance was able to put an estimate on the loss of revenue on these three items. At page 1216 of Hansard, referring to this particular proposal, he says;
We have received strong representations from the dairy interests that the removal of this tax will give encouragement to the consumption of ice cream and dairy drinks at a time when sales of certain other milk products are declining. The loss of revenue in this item will be about $2 million in a full year.
I submitted an inquiry some weeks ago to the following effect:
What amounts have been collected, by years, and in the aggregate, by way of sales tax from the outset of levy thereof on (a) ice cream; (b) other foods; (c) clothing; (d) household furniture?
The answer submitted by the Minister of National Revenue was, to say the least, cryptic. It said:
Information not available. No separate statistics are maintained of sales tax collected on individual commodities.
Nevertheless it has been possible for the Minister of Finance, on giving some thought to this question, to put an estimate on the actual loss of revenue to be anticipated from the removal of the sales tax on these three particular commodities. It seems to me, since the Minister of Finance is in a position to do that, the Minister of National Revenue should be in a position at least to give some information in reply to the inquiries that I submitted; and I wonder if it is still not the intention of the department to submit the information in reply to the questions asked about the other foods.

I am not going to risk your disapproval by saying anything about the subject of clothing or household furniture. I am confining myself strictly to the subject of prepared foods, of which these are examples.

Mr. Chairman, the principal reason, of course, why these three prepared foods have now been made exempt, where there are still a variety of prepared foods such as pickles, catsup, sauces, olives, horseradish, mustard and so forth still not exempt, or mainly excluded, is that demands have been made by farmer members of this hoo'e for further aid to their industry. That was the advice given by the minister, and it is the advice that was given nere a little earlier on the same thing.
The actual list of these prepared foods which are still not sales tax exempt is a fairly small one, and they are not of the types which are nominally regarded by the average family as being essen'ial for their daily diet. These foods are commonly used, but what apparently is more importani to the farmer members of this house is that it gives a little more encouragement to the dairy industry.

Is the list of foods the parliamentary assistant has ju=t read a complete list of the foods on which sales tax is still levied?
Excise Tax Act Amendment

No. They are under the one heading here. I think if hon. members will study their own lists they will find therein not very many of the ordinary foods. I think there are none of the ordinary foods and not very many of the more special types here that are not exempt from sales tax, and certainly the inclusion of these three is a thing which will be welcomed not only by the farmers of the country but by the people generally.

Resolution agreed to.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will go into committee of ways and means, and continue the consideration of these resolutions. If they pass, we will go into supply and take up the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
May I ask in which order the remaining resolutions will be taken up, income tax and then customs, or vice versa?
Income tax next, and then customs.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, April 28, 1950
